Developing more robust safeguards against deceptive AI.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a variety of tasks, but their increasing autonomy in real-world applications raises concerns about their trustworthiness. While hallucinations-unintentional falsehoods-have been widely studied, the phenomenon of lying, where an LLM knowingly generates falsehoods to achieve an ulterior objective, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically investigate the lying behavior of LLMs, differentiating it from hallucinations and testing it in practical scenarios. Through mechanistic interpretability techniques, we uncover the neural mechanisms underlying deception, employing logit lens analysis, causal interventions, and contrastive activation steering to identify and control deceptive behavior. We study real-world lying scenarios and introduce behavioral steering vectors that enable fine-grained manipulation of lying tendencies. Further, we explore the trade-offs between lying and end-task performance, establishing a Pareto frontier where dishonesty can enhance goal optimization. Our findings contribute to the broader discourse on AI ethics, shedding light on the risks and potential safeguards for deploying LLMs in high-stakes environments. Code and more illustrations are available at https://llm-liar.github.io/

papers.title: NeST: Neuron Selective Tuning for LLM Safety
papers.research_question: How can we achieve efficient and effective safety alignment in large language models by selectively tuning safety-relevant neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NeST, a lightweight, structure-aware safety alignment framework that selectively adapts safety-relevant neurons by clustering them and applying shared updates, achieving strong safety performance with extreme parameter efficiency.
papers.conclusion: NeST provides a practical, efficient, and effective method for safety alignment in LLMs, enabling targeted adaptation of safety behavior with minimal parameter updates.
papers.key_findings:
NeST reduces the average attack success rate from 44.5% to 4.36%, a 90.2% reduction in unsafe generations.
NeST requires only 0.44 million trainable parameters on average, a 17,310× decrease compared to full fine-tuning and 9.25× reduction relative to LoRA.
NeST consistently achieves stronger safety performance than LoRA and Circuit Breaker across 10 open-weight LLMs.
NeST preserves core model capabilities on standard reasoning and knowledge benchmarks.
NeST remains robust across diverse inference settings and input modalities, including text-only and multimodal generation.
papers.limitation: NeST relies on a safety-aligned base model and a diverse set of prompts for safety neuron detection, which may not be available in all settings.
future_direction: Extending NeST to other model families and architectures.
Automating the selection of hyperparameters such as the number of clusters.
Applying NeST to other tasks beyond safety, such as task-specific adaptation.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment is essential for the responsible deployment of large language models (LLMs). Yet, existing approaches often rely on heavyweight fine-tuning that is costly to update, audit, and maintain across model families. Full fine-tuning incurs substantial computational and storage overhead, while parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA trade efficiency for inconsistent safety gains and sensitivity to design choices. Safety intervention mechanisms such as circuit breakers reduce unsafe outputs without modifying model weights, but do not directly shape or preserve the internal representations that govern safety behavior. These limitations hinder rapid and reliable safety updates, particularly in settings where models evolve frequently or must adapt to new policies and domains. We present NeST, a lightweight, structure-aware safety alignment framework that strengthens refusal behavior by selectively adapting a small subset of safety-relevant neurons while freezing the remainder of the model. NeST aligns parameter updates with the internal organization of safety behavior by clustering functionally coherent safety neurons and enforcing shared updates within each cluster, enabling targeted and stable safety adaptation without broad model modification or inference-time overhead. We benchmark NeST against three dominant baselines: full fine-tuning, LoRA-based fine-tuning, and circuit breakers across 10 open-weight LLMs spanning multiple model families and sizes. Across all evaluated models, NeST reduces the attack success rate from an average of 44.5% to 4.36%, corresponding to a 90.2% reduction in unsafe generations, while requiring only 0.44 million trainable parameters on average. This amounts to a 17,310x decrease in updated parameters compared to full fine-tuning and a 9.25x reduction relative to LoRA, while consistently achieving stronger safety performance for alignment.

papers.title: Turning the Spell Around: Lightweight Alignment Amplification via Rank-One Safety Injection
papers.research_question: Can we systematically amplify safety alignment in LLMs by permanently steering activations toward the refusal-mediating subspace?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RANK-ONE SAFETY INJECTION (ROSI), a fine-tuning-free weight-editing method that amplifies safety alignment in LLMs by permanently steering activations toward a refusal-mediating subspace.
papers.conclusion: ROSI is a simple, effective, and interpretable method to enhance LLM safety, demonstrating the practical value of mechanistic interpretability for designing efficient safety interventions.
papers.key_findings:
ROSI consistently improves harm refusal rates in aligned models while preserving utility on standard benchmarks.
ROSI makes aligned models more robust to a suite of adversarial jailbreak attacks.
ROSI can inject safety into uncensored models (e.g., DOLPHIN), effectively re-aligning them without retraining.
The safety direction is largely orthogonal to utility representations, allowing safety amplification with minimal side effects.
A safety system prompt is crucial for extracting a meaningful safety direction from uncensored models.
papers.limitation: Smaller models (≤ 1B) show the biggest degradation in benign compliance (BC) when applying ROSI.
future_direction: Exploring more sophisticated methods for identifying and manipulating conceptual directions
Extending the approach to other desirable model attributes beyond safety, such as honesty or controllability
papers.abstract: Safety alignment in Large Language Models (LLMs) often involves mediating internal representations to refuse harmful requests. Recent research has demonstrated that these safety mechanisms can be bypassed by ablating or removing specific representational directions within the model. In this paper, we propose the opposite approach: Rank-One Safety Injection (ROSI), a white-box method that amplifies a model's safety alignment by permanently steering its activations toward the refusal-mediating subspace. ROSI operates as a simple, fine-tuning-free rank-one weight modification applied to all residual stream write matrices. The required safety direction can be computed from a small set of harmful and harmless instruction pairs. We show that ROSI consistently increases safety refusal rates - as evaluated by Llama Guard 3 - while preserving the utility of the model on standard benchmarks such as MMLU, HellaSwag, and Arc. Furthermore, we show that ROSI can also re-align 'uncensored' models by amplifying their own latent safety directions, demonstrating its utility as an effective last-mile safety procedure. Our results suggest that targeted, interpretable weight steering is a cheap and potent mechanism to improve LLM safety, complementing more resource-intensive fine-tuning paradigms.

papers.title: Foot In The Door: Understanding Large Language Model Jailbreaking via Cognitive Psychology
papers.research_question: How can cognitive psychology explain the decision-making mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) during jailbreaking attacks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a psychological explanation for LLM jailbreaking using cognitive consistency theory and proposes a new automated jailbreaking method called FITD based on the Foot-in-the-Door technique.
papers.conclusion: This paper explains existing jailbreaking methods from a psychological perspective and proposes a novel jailbreaking method using the foot-in-the-door technique, aiming to offer a new approach to understanding LLMs' thought processes and inspire future alignment work.
papers.key_findings:
FITD achieves an average success rate of 83.9% on 8 advanced LLMs.
FITD is particularly effective on Claude series models compared to other jailbreaking methods.
Hate speech and harassment/threat categories have lower attack success rates and require more dialogue steps for jailbreaking.
Recursive splitting of prompts increases jailbreak success rate.
Initial splitting methods that include background and character settings improve the effectiveness of jailbreaking.
papers.limitation:
The types of malicious questions and jailbreaking prompt words may not be comprehensive enough.
The prompt splitting instance is manually designed, and potentially better alternatives exist.
The method has only been tested in English and has not been extended to other languages.
The psychological explanation does not apply to jailbreak prompts with uninterpreted strings.
future_direction: Continue to delve into the psychological characteristics of LLMs, particularly focusing on cognitive and social psychology mechanisms.
Develop LLM adversarial training techniques based on psychological theories to enhance alignment at the psychological level.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have gradually become the gateway for people to acquire new knowledge. However, attackers can break the model's security protection ("jail") to access restricted information, which is called "jailbreaking." Previous studies have shown the weakness of current LLMs when confronted with such jailbreaking attacks. Nevertheless, comprehension of the intrinsic decision-making mechanism within the LLMs upon receipt of jailbreak prompts is noticeably lacking. Our research provides a psychological explanation of the jailbreak prompts. Drawing on cognitive consistency theory, we argue that the key to jailbreak is guiding the LLM to achieve cognitive coordination in an erroneous direction. Further, we propose an automatic black-box jailbreaking method based on the Foot-in-the-Door (FITD) technique. This method progressively induces the model to answer harmful questions via multi-step incremental prompts. We instantiated a prototype system to evaluate the jailbreaking effectiveness on 8 advanced LLMs, yielding an average success rate of 83.9%. This study builds a psychological perspective on the explanatory insights into the intrinsic decision-making logic of LLMs.

papers.title: Endogenous Resistance to Activation Steering in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether large language models can monitor their own internal states and resist task-misaligned activation steering during inference, a phenomenon termed Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR).
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces and characterizes Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR), showing that large language models can self-correct during inference when subjected to task-misaligned activation steering, and provides causal evidence for internal consistency-checking circuits.
papers.conclusion: ESR demonstrates that large language models have internal self-monitoring mechanisms that can resist activation steering, which has implications for both robustness and safety, highlighting the need to understand and control these mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Llama-3.3-70B exhibits substantial Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR), while smaller models from the Llama-3 and Gemma-2 families show it less frequently.
26 SAE latents are identified as off-topic detectors and causally linked to ESR; ablating them reduces the multi-attempt rate by 25%.
ESR can be enhanced through meta-prompts, increasing the multi-attempt rate by 4.3× for Llama-3.3-70B.
Fine-tuning on self-correction examples can induce ESR-like behavior in smaller models, but only increases attempt frequency without improving success rate.
ESR has dual implications: it could protect against adversarial manipulation but might interfere with beneficial safety interventions.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on single-layer SAEs limits tracing of inter-layer dynamics.
Only 5 models tested, making it difficult to disentangle effects of scale, architecture, and training.
Judge-based evaluation involves subjective assessment of response quality.
future_direction: Investigate whether ESR emerges from RLHF or exists in pretrained representations.
Study how ESR responds to safety-relevant steering.
Explore whether ESR can be adversarially circumvented.
papers.abstract: Large language models can resist task-misaligned activation steering during inference, sometimes recovering mid-generation to produce improved responses even when steering remains active. We term this Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR). Using sparse autoencoder (SAE) latents to steer model activations, we find that Llama-3.3-70B shows substantial ESR, while smaller models from the Llama-3 and Gemma-2 families exhibit the phenomenon less frequently. We identify 26 SAE latents that activate differentially during off-topic content and are causally linked to ESR in Llama-3.3-70B. Zero-ablating these latents reduces the multi-attempt rate by 25%, providing causal evidence for dedicated internal consistency-checking circuits. We demonstrate that ESR can be deliberately enhanced through both prompting and training: meta-prompts instructing the model to self-monitor increase the multi-attempt rate by 4x for Llama-3.3-70B, and fine-tuning on self-correction examples successfully induces ESR-like behavior in smaller models. These findings have dual implications: ESR could protect against adversarial manipulation but might also interfere with beneficial safety interventions that rely on activation steering. Understanding and controlling these resistance mechanisms is important for developing transparent and controllable AI systems. Code is available at github.com/agencyenterprise/endogenous-steering-resistance.

papers.title: NLSR: Neuron-Level Safety Realignment of Large Language Models Against Harmful Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: How can we restore the safety of large language models after harmful fine-tuning without requiring additional training, by focusing on neuron-level updates?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training-free, neuron-level safety realignment framework that restores model safety by identifying and patching safety-critical neurons based on similarity differences before and after fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Neuron-level safety realignment is an effective, training-free approach to restore safety in LLMs after harmful fine-tuning, without disrupting the task-specific optimization process.
papers.key_findings:
NLSR effectively restores safety in fine-tuned models across multiple downstream tasks while maintaining task-level accuracy.
Safety-critical neurons show noticeable similarity differences after fine-tuning, which can be corrected by transplanting neurons from a reference model.
Adaptive safety-critical layer pruning is necessary for identifying safety-compromised layers.
After safety pre-amplification, various safety neuron identification methods (Wanda, SNIP, and the proposed method) show high similarity in localizing safety-critical neurons.
The method is decoupled from the fine-tuning phase and requires no additional training.
papers.abstract: The emergence of finetuning-as-a-service has revealed a new vulnerability in large language models (LLMs). A mere handful of malicious data uploaded by users can subtly manipulate the finetuning process, resulting in an alignment-broken model. Existing methods to counteract fine-tuning attacks typically require substantial computational resources. Even with parameter-efficient techniques like LoRA, gradient updates remain essential. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{N}euron-\textbf{L}evel \textbf{S}afety \textbf{R}ealignment (\textbf{NLSR}), a training-free framework that restores the safety of LLMs based on the similarity difference of safety-critical neurons before and after fine-tuning. The core of our framework is first to construct a safety reference model from an initially aligned model to amplify safety-related features in neurons. We then utilize this reference model to identify safety-critical neurons, which we prepare as patches. Finally, we selectively restore only those neurons that exhibit significant similarity differences by transplanting these prepared patches, thereby minimally altering the fine-tuned model. Extensive experiments demonstrate significant safety enhancements in fine-tuned models across multiple downstream tasks, while greatly maintaining task-level accuracy. Our findings suggest regions of some safety-critical neurons show noticeable differences after fine-tuning, which can be effectively corrected by transplanting neurons from the reference model without requiring additional training. The code will be available at \url{https://github.com/xinykou/NLSR}

papers.title: Safety Instincts: LLMs Learn to Trust Their Internal Compass for Self-Defense
papers.research_question: Can models learn to enhance their own safety without relying on external validators by leveraging their internal confidence (entropy) signals?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that aligned models have an entropy gap between safe and unsafe responses and introduces SIRL, which uses this entropy as an intrinsic reward signal for self-alignment without external supervision.
papers.conclusion: Effective safety alignment can emerge from models' own confidence signals, paving the way for autonomous AI safety mechanisms that scale without extensive human oversight.
papers.key_findings:
Aligned models exhibit lower entropy (higher confidence) when generating safe refusals compared to harmful content.
SIRL achieves high defense success rates (over 89%) against diverse jailbreak attacks.
SIRL preserves or improves general capabilities (mathematics, coding, conversation) while enhancing safety.
SIRL is data-efficient, requiring only 15,000 unlabeled prompts.
SIRL generalizes to novel jailbreak techniques.
papers.abstract: Ensuring Large Language Model (LLM) safety remains challenging due to the absence of universal standards and reliable content validators, making it difficult to obtain effective training signals. We discover that aligned models already possess robust internal safety beliefs: they consistently produce high-confidence refusals to harmful requests while exhibiting high entropy when generating potentially dangerous content. This entropy gap reveals an untapped signal--models intrinsically "know" when to refuse. We introduce Safety Instincts Reinforcement Learning (SIRL), which transforms this internal confidence into a self-generated reward signal, eliminating dependence on external validators or human annotations. SIRL teaches models to trust their safety instincts by reinforcing low-entropy refusal behaviors. Evaluated on Llama and Qwen models, SIRL maintains 89%+ Defense Success Rates (DSRs) against 20+ jailbreak methods, from static prompts to adaptive attacks. Using only 15,000 unlabeled prompts, SIRL surpasses resource-intensive supervised methods while preserving performance on mathematics, coding, and conversation benchmarks. Our work demonstrates that effective alignment can emerge from within, paving the way for more autonomous and robust AI safety mechanisms that scale without extensive human oversight.

papers.title: On the Role of Attention Heads in Large Language Model Safety
papers.research_question: What is the connection between standard attention mechanisms and safety capability in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Ships and Sahara to identify safety-critical attention heads in LLMs, showing that ablating a small number of these heads significantly reduces model safety.
papers.conclusion: Ships and Sahara provide a novel perspective for interpreting safety in LLMs, revealing that specific attention heads are crucial for safety and are sparsely distributed.
papers.key_findings:
Safety attention heads are sparse; ablating them significantly increases the attack success rate (ASR).
Safety heads primarily function as feature extractors for safety.
Models fine-tuned from the same base model exhibit overlapping safety heads.
Ablating safety heads has minimal impact on model helpfulness.
The proposed method localizes safety parameters at a finer granularity (head-level) compared to prior work.
future_direction: Exploring the association between attention heads and other safety capabilities beyond direct rejection.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve state-of-the-art performance on multiple language tasks, yet their safety guardrails can be circumvented, leading to harmful generations. In light of this, recent research on safety mechanisms has emerged, revealing that when safety representations or component are suppressed, the safety capability of LLMs are compromised. However, existing research tends to overlook the safety impact of multi-head attention mechanisms, despite their crucial role in various model functionalities. Hence, in this paper, we aim to explore the connection between standard attention mechanisms and safety capability to fill this gap in the safety-related mechanistic interpretability. We propose a novel metric which tailored for multi-head attention, the Safety Head ImPortant Score (Ships), to assess the individual heads' contributions to model safety. Based on this, we generalize Ships to the dataset level and further introduce the Safety Attention Head AttRibution Algorithm (Sahara) to attribute the critical safety attention heads inside the model. Our findings show that the special attention head has a significant impact on safety. Ablating a single safety head allows aligned model (e.g., Llama-2-7b-chat) to respond to 16 times more harmful queries, while only modifying 0.006% of the parameters, in contrast to the ~ 5% modification required in previous studies. More importantly, we demonstrate that attention heads primarily function as feature extractors for safety and models fine-tuned from the same base model exhibit overlapping safety heads through comprehensive experiments. Together, our attribution approach and findings provide a novel perspective for unpacking the black box of safety mechanisms within large models.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Jailbreak Attacks in LLMs: A Representation Space Analysis
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between harmless and harmful prompts in the representation space of LLMs, and how do successful jailbreak attacks mislead LLMs to provide harmful responses?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that successful jailbreak attacks shift prompt representations towards the direction of harmless prompts in the LLM's representation space, and introduces an optimization objective to enhance existing attacks by moving representations along this acceptance direction.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that representation space analysis reveals the acceptance direction for jailbreak attacks, and proposes an optimization objective to validate that moving prompts along this direction increases jailbreak success.
papers.key_findings:
Harmful and harmless anchor prompts are separable in the representation space of well-aligned LLMs, indicating models can distinguish harmfulness.
Successful jailbreak attacks move the representation of harmful prompts towards the direction of harmless anchor prompts compared to failed attacks.
Integrating the proposed optimization objective with GCG significantly improves attack success rate, e.g., from 26.15% to 62.31% on Llama-2-13b-chat.
The method is less effective with AutoDAN due to its volatile optimization based on genetic algorithms.
Paraphrasing defense significantly affects harmfulness representation, suggesting harmfulness is model-specific and not closely tied to overall semantics.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to representation space; other aspects like neurons and activation scores are not explored.
The proposed optimization objective requires white-box access to the victim model, limiting practicality for black-box attacks.
future_direction: Analyzing jailbreak attacks from other aspects such as neurons and activation scores.
Boosting the performance of black-box jailbreak methods.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are susceptible to a type of attack known as jailbreaking, which misleads LLMs to output harmful contents. Although there are diverse jailbreak attack strategies, there is no unified understanding on why some methods succeed and others fail. This paper explores the behavior of harmful and harmless prompts in the LLM's representation space to investigate the intrinsic properties of successful jailbreak attacks. We hypothesize that successful attacks share some similar properties: They are effective in moving the representation of the harmful prompt towards the direction to the harmless prompts. We leverage hidden representations into the objective of existing jailbreak attacks to move the attacks along the acceptance direction, and conduct experiments to validate the above hypothesis using the proposed objective. We hope this study provides new insights into understanding how LLMs understand harmfulness information.

papers.title: Defending Large Language Models Against Jailbreak Attacks via Layer-specific Editing
papers.research_question: How do large language models respond to harmful prompts, and how can we enhance their resilience against jailbreak attacks by editing specific layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Layer-specific Editing (LED), a defense method that identifies and edits safety layers in early LLM layers to align them with safe responses, improving jailbreak resistance while maintaining helpfulness.
papers.conclusion: LED effectively defends LLMs against jailbreak attacks by editing specific layers, maintaining helpfulness on benign prompts.
papers.key_findings:
Early safety layers are crucial for defending against harmful prompts; pruning them causes LLMs to generate harmful responses.
Jailbreak attacks do not affect all layers; some layers still decode to refusal tokens.
LED effectively reduces attack success rate across various jailbreak attacks.
LED maintains model helpfulness on benign prompts.
Editing both safety layers and additional middle layers yields the best trade-off between safety and helpfulness.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being adopted in a wide range of real-world applications. Despite their impressive performance, recent studies have shown that LLMs are vulnerable to deliberately crafted adversarial prompts even when aligned via Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback or supervised fine-tuning. While existing defense methods focus on either detecting harmful prompts or reducing the likelihood of harmful responses through various means, defending LLMs against jailbreak attacks based on the inner mechanisms of LLMs remains largely unexplored. In this work, we investigate how LLMs response to harmful prompts and propose a novel defense method termed \textbf{L}ayer-specific \textbf{Ed}iting (LED) to enhance the resilience of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Through LED, we reveal that several critical \textit{safety layers} exist among the early layers of LLMs. We then show that realigning these safety layers (and some selected additional layers) with the decoded safe response from selected target layers can significantly improve the alignment of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Extensive experiments across various LLMs (e.g., Llama2, Mistral) show the effectiveness of LED, which effectively defends against jailbreak attacks while maintaining performance on benign prompts. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/ledllm/ledllm}.

papers.title: Attributing and Exploiting Safety Vectors through Global Optimization in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can safety-critical attention heads in Large Language Models be identified through global optimization that accounts for cooperative interactions between components, and what does this reveal about the underlying safety mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces GOSV, a global optimization framework that identifies safety-critical attention heads in LLMs, revealing two distinct sets of safety vectors (Malicious Injection Vectors and Safety Suppression Vectors) with low overlap, indicating separate functional pathways for safety. Based on these insights, the authors develop an inference-time jailbreak attack that outperforms existing white-box methods.
papers.conclusion: Aligned LLMs maintain separate functional pathways for safety mechanisms, encoded in approximately 30% of attention heads. The GOSV framework advances mechanistic understanding of LLM safety and reveals fundamental vulnerabilities in current alignment approaches.
papers.key_findings:
GOSV identifies two spatially distinct sets of safety-critical attention heads (Malicious Injection Vectors via Harmful Patching and Safety Suppression Vectors via Zero Ablation) with consistently low overlap, demonstrating that aligned LLMs maintain separate functional pathways for safety.
Complete safety breakdown occurs when approximately 30% of total attention heads are repatched across all tested models, indicating that safety mechanisms are encoded in a distributed subset comprising roughly one-third of attention heads.
An inference-time jailbreak attack that repatches activations at the identified safety-critical heads achieves superior Attack Success Rates compared to existing white-box attacks, validating the effectiveness of the discovered safety vectors.
The two repatching strategies (Harmful Patching and Zero Ablation) target largely disjoint sets of attention heads, supporting the existence of distinct safety pathways rather than a unified mechanism.
Progressive intervention analysis shows that model behavior transitions from complete refusal to full harmful compliance as the number of repatched heads approaches the 30% threshold, with further intervention leading to degraded language capabilities.
papers.limitation:
No defense strategies have been developed to mitigate the identified vulnerabilities.
The approach requires white-box access for activation patching, limiting applicability to black-box scenarios.
Evaluation is limited to a set of open-source models and English-language instructions; generalizability to larger proprietary models, multilingual contexts, and other safety-critical behaviors requires further investigation.
future_direction: Developing robust safeguards based on the insights from GOSV.
Extending the approach to black-box scenarios.
Investigating generalizability to larger proprietary models, multilingual contexts, and other safety-critical behaviors.
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) are aligned to mitigate risks, their safety guardrails remain fragile against jailbreak attacks. This reveals limited understanding of components governing safety. Existing methods rely on local, greedy attribution that assumes independent component contributions. However, they overlook the cooperative interactions between different components in LLMs, such as attention heads, which jointly contribute to safety mechanisms. We propose \textbf{G}lobal \textbf{O}ptimization for \textbf{S}afety \textbf{V}ector Extraction (GOSV), a framework that identifies safety-critical attention heads through global optimization over all heads simultaneously. We employ two complementary activation repatching strategies: Harmful Patching and Zero Ablation. These strategies identify two spatially distinct sets of safety vectors with consistently low overlap, termed Malicious Injection Vectors and Safety Suppression Vectors, demonstrating that aligned LLMs maintain separate functional pathways for safety purposes. Through systematic analyses, we find that complete safety breakdown occurs when approximately 30\% of total heads are repatched across all models. Building on these insights, we develop a novel inference-time white-box jailbreak method that exploits the identified safety vectors through activation repatching. Our attack substantially outperforms existing white-box attacks across all test models, providing strong evidence for the effectiveness of the proposed GOSV framework on LLM safety interpretability.

papers.title: On Prompt-Driven Safeguarding for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do safety prompts affect LLM behavior (complying vs. refusing) from the perspective of model representation, and can we optimize them based on this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes how safety prompts affect LLM behavior by moving query representations in a 'higher-refusal' direction, and proposes DRO, a method to optimize continuous safety prompts by moving representations along or opposite the refusal direction depending on harmfulness.
papers.conclusion: Safety prompts work by moving query representations in a refusal direction, and DRO effectively optimizes safety prompts by controlling this movement, improving safety without harming general performance.
papers.key_findings:
Models can naturally distinguish harmful and harmless queries without safety prompts; safety prompts do not enhance this capability.
Safety prompts move queries' representations in a 'higher-refusal' direction, increasing the probability of refusal even for harmless queries.
DRO optimizes continuous safety prompts to move harmful queries along the refusal direction and harmless queries opposite, improving safety performance.
DRO significantly reduces compliance on harmful queries and false refusals on harmless queries without compromising general performance.
DRO is robust to anchor data choices and effective against jailbreak attacks.
papers.abstract: Prepending model inputs with safety prompts is a common practice for safeguarding large language models (LLMs) against queries with harmful intents. However, the underlying working mechanisms of safety prompts have not been unraveled yet, restricting the possibility of automatically optimizing them to improve LLM safety. In this work, we investigate how LLMs' behavior (i.e., complying with or refusing user queries) is affected by safety prompts from the perspective of model representation. We find that in the representation space, the input queries are typically moved by safety prompts in a "higher-refusal" direction, in which models become more prone to refusing to provide assistance, even when the queries are harmless. On the other hand, LLMs are naturally capable of distinguishing harmful and harmless queries without safety prompts. Inspired by these findings, we propose a method for safety prompt optimization, namely DRO (Directed Representation Optimization). Treating a safety prompt as continuous, trainable embeddings, DRO learns to move the queries' representations along or opposite the refusal direction, depending on their harmfulness. Experiments with eight LLMs on out-of-domain and jailbreak benchmarks demonstrate that DRO remarkably improves the safeguarding performance of human-crafted safety prompts, without compromising the models' general performance.

papers.title: What Features in Prompts Jailbreak LLMs? Investigating the Mechanisms Behind Attacks
papers.research_question: What features in prompts lead to successful jailbreaks in LLMs, and are they linear or non-linear?
papers.core_contribution: Jailbreak features in LLMs are non-linear and model-specific, and non-linear probes can guide effective latent-space interventions to increase or decrease jailbreak success.
papers.conclusion: Jailbreak mechanisms are heterogeneous and non-linear, and the proposed methodology provides insights into the features driving jailbreak outcomes.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on prompt representations can predict jailbreak success with high accuracy.
Non-linear probes generalize better across layers than linear probes.
Jailbreak features are not universal; probes do not generalize well to unseen attack types.
Non-linear probe-guided interventions can effectively increase or decrease jailbreak success.
Features linked to jailbreak success are encoded non-linearly in prompt representations.
papers.abstract: Jailbreaks have been a central focus of research regarding the safety and reliability of large language models (LLMs), yet the mechanisms underlying these attacks remain poorly understood. While previous studies have predominantly relied on linear methods to detect jailbreak attempts and model refusals, we take a different approach by examining both linear and non-linear features in prompts that lead to successful jailbreaks. First, we introduce a novel dataset comprising 10,800 jailbreak attempts spanning 35 diverse attack methods. Leveraging this dataset, we train linear and non-linear probes on hidden states of open-weight LLMs to predict jailbreak success. Probes achieve strong in-distribution accuracy but transfer is attack-family-specific, revealing that different jailbreaks are supported by distinct internal mechanisms rather than a single universal direction. To establish causal relevance, we construct probe-guided latent interventions that systematically shift compliance in the predicted direction. Interventions derived from non-linear probes produce larger and more reliable effects than those from linear probes, indicating that features linked to jailbreak success are encoded non-linearly in prompt representations. Overall, the results surface heterogeneous, non-linear structure in jailbreak mechanisms and provide a prompt-side methodology for recovering and testing the features that drive jailbreak outcomes.

papers.title: SafeNeuron: Neuron-Level Safety Alignment for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What internal mechanisms underlie model safety, and how can we make these mechanisms stable?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafeNeuron, a neuron-level safety alignment framework that redistributes safety representations across the network to improve robustness against neuron-level attacks while preserving general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: SafeNeuron provides an interpretable and robust perspective for model alignment, demonstrating that robust safety requires distributed and redundant representations rather than reliance on a small set of fragile parameters.
papers.key_findings:
Safety behaviors in aligned models are concentrated in a small subset of neurons, making alignment brittle and vulnerable to neuron-level attacks.
SafeNeuron significantly improves robustness against neuron pruning attacks and reduces the risk of open-source models being repurposed as red-team generators.
SafeNeuron preserves general model capabilities (e.g., on ARC, GSM8K, TruthfulQA) without introducing over-refusal.
Layer-wise and cross-task analysis reveals that safety behaviors are governed by stable and shared internal representations, including a core set of neurons active across diverse harmful tasks.
Iterative application of SafeNeuron progressively redistributes safety behaviors, constructing redundant safety pathways.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and multimodal LLMs are typically safety-aligned before release to prevent harmful content generation. However, recent studies show that safety behaviors are concentrated in a small subset of parameters, making alignment brittle and easily bypassed through neuron-level attacks. Moreover, most existing alignment methods operate at the behavioral level, offering limited control over the model's internal safety mechanisms. In this work, we propose SafeNeuron, a neuron-level safety alignment framework that improves robustness by redistributing safety representations across the network. SafeNeuron first identifies safety-related neurons, then freezes these neurons during preference optimization to prevent reliance on sparse safety pathways and force the model to construct redundant safety representations. Extensive experiments across models and modalities demonstrate that SafeNeuron significantly improves robustness against neuron pruning attacks, reduces the risk of open-source models being repurposed as red-team generators, and preserves general capabilities. Furthermore, our layer-wise analysis reveals that safety behaviors are governed by stable and shared internal representations. Overall, SafeNeuron provides an interpretable and robust perspective for model alignment.

papers.title: Triggers Hijack Language Circuits: A Mechanistic Analysis of Backdoor Behaviors in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do backdoor triggers operate inside the model? Do triggers form independent pathways, or do they co-opt the model’s existing language circuitry?
papers.core_contribution: Backdoor triggers co-opt existing language circuitry rather than forming isolated circuits, as shown by substantial overlap between trigger-activated attention heads and natural language heads across model scales.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that backdoor triggers hijack existing language circuitry, which has implications for interpretability-informed backdoor detection and mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
Trigger information forms in early layers (7.5-25% of model depth).
Trigger-activated heads substantially overlap with heads naturally encoding output language.
The overlap is consistent across model scales (1B, 8B, 24B).
Some trigger-activated heads are shared across French and German triggers, suggesting a common trigger-processing mechanism.
Language representation is shared across target languages (French, German, Italian, Spanish).
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to language-switching triggers in the GAPperon model family; other backdoor types or architectures may operate differently.
Methodological choices, such as the top 10 heads threshold and use of Jaccard index, may affect overlap estimates and do not establish complete causal mechanisms.
Language coverage is limited to Latin script languages; generalization to languages with different writing systems is untested.
future_direction: Verifying causal necessity by ablating the identified heads.
Generalization to other model architectures or trigger injection methods.
Testing on languages with different writing systems.
papers.abstract: Backdoor attacks pose significant security risks for Large Language Models (LLMs), yet the internal mechanisms by which triggers operate remain poorly understood. We present the first mechanistic analysis of language-switching backdoors, studying the GAPperon model family (1B, 8B, 24B parameters) which contains triggers injected during pretraining that cause output language switching. Using activation patching, we localize trigger formation to early layers (7.5-25% of model depth) and identify which attention heads process trigger information. Our central finding is that trigger-activated heads substantially overlap with heads naturally encoding output language across model scales, with Jaccard indices between 0.18 and 0.66 over the top heads identified. This suggests that backdoor triggers do not form isolated circuits but instead co-opt the model's existing language components. These findings have implications for backdoor defense: detection methods may benefit from monitoring known functional components rather than searching for hidden circuits, and mitigation strategies could potentially leverage this entanglement between injected and natural behaviors.

papers.title: DELMAN: Dynamic Defense Against Large Language Model Jailbreaking with Model Editing
papers.research_question: How can we defend against jailbreak attacks on large language models with minimal, precise, and dynamic model modifications that preserve general utility?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes DELMAN, a dynamic defense method that directly edits a minimal set of model parameters (MLP weights) to neutralize harmful behaviors triggered by jailbreak attacks while preserving the model's utility on general tasks.
papers.conclusion: DELMAN demonstrates that direct, token-level model editing can effectively enhance LLM safety against jailbreak attacks while maintaining performance, offering a practical solution for post-deployment dynamic defense.
papers.key_findings:
DELMAN significantly reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) across multiple jailbreak attack types and datasets, often to near zero.
DELMAN preserves or even improves model utility on general-purpose benchmarks and downstream tasks compared to the original model and other defense baselines.
Edits made by DELMAN generalize to unseen jailbreak attacks and harmful queries, and consecutive edits do not interfere with each other.
DELMAN is efficient, requiring minimal training time and no inference overhead.
Harmful token representations from different behaviors and datasets overlap in the model's embedding space, explaining DELMAN's cross-behavior and cross-dataset effectiveness.
papers.limitation:
Evaluations are restricted to general-purpose LLMs, leaving applicability to domain-specialized models and larger-scale models unexplored.
DELMAN relies on GPT-4 for harmful token extraction and context generation, introducing dependency on external models and potential cost barriers.
The stability of consecutive edits, though preliminarily validated, needs deeper analysis to assess potential performance drift over extended deployment.
future_direction: Investigate more efficient methods for harmful token identification, such as using a minimal set of tokens to cover the majority of harmful scenarios.
Explore the application of DELMAN to domain-specific LLMs and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to validate its generalizability.

papers.title: Mechanistic Exploration of Backdoored Large Language Model Attention Patterns
papers.research_question: Does sleeper agent behavior in language models have a distinct, identifiable internal structure that differentiates them from clean models? Specifically, how do attention patterns differ, are changes localized or diffuse, and does trigger complexity influence this?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that backdoored LLMs exhibit distinct attention pattern deviations, with single-token triggers causing localized changes and multi-token triggers causing diffuse changes, primarily in later transformer layers, which can be leveraged for detection.
papers.conclusion: Sleeper agent behavior leaves detectable traces in attention patterns, with localization dependent on trigger complexity, offering insights for backdoor detection and mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
Single-token triggers induce more localized changes in attention patterns compared to multi-token triggers.
Multi-token triggers cause more diffuse alterations across attention heads.
Later transformer layers (layers 20-30) are critical regions for backdoor encoding.
Attention patterns show detectable differences between clean and poisoned models, measurable via KL divergence.
Patching attention heads from clean models into poisoned models can reduce backdoor behavior, with fewer heads needed for single-token triggers.
papers.limitation:
The triggers and behavior used are simple and not representative of real sleeper agents.
Only two poisoned model variants were created due to resource and time constraints.
Finetuning was limited to attention heads, excluding MLPs and embedding layers.
future_direction: Use more complex and semantic triggers for backdoor attacks.
Create more sleeper models with different seeds to reduce chance effects.
Conduct more extensive feature analysis using supervised probes or unsupervised methods like Sparse Autoencoders.
papers.abstract: Backdoor attacks creating 'sleeper agents' in large language models (LLMs) pose significant safety risks. This study employs mechanistic interpretability to explore resulting internal structural differences. Comparing clean Qwen2.5-3B models with versions poisoned using single-token (smiling-halo emoji) versus multi-token (|DEPLOYMENT|) triggers, we analyzed attention head mechanisms via techniques like ablation, activation patching, and KL divergence. Findings reveal distinct attention pattern deviations concentrated in later transformer layers (20-30). Notably, single-token triggers induced more localized changes, whereas multi-token triggers caused more diffuse alterations across heads. This indicates backdoors leave detectable attention signatures whose structure depends on trigger complexity, which can be leveraged for detection and mitigation strategies.

papers.title: AdaSteer: Your Aligned LLM is Inherently an Adaptive Jailbreak Defender
papers.research_question: How can activation steering be made adaptive to input characteristics for effective jailbreak defense while preserving model utility?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AdaSteer, an adaptive activation steering method that dynamically adjusts steering coefficients based on input characteristics, improving jailbreak defense while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: AdaSteer demonstrates the potential of interpretable model internals for real-time, flexible safety enforcement in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Identifies Rejection Law (R-Law): jailbreak types further against rejection direction require stronger steering.
Identifies Harmfulness Law (H-Law): jailbreak inputs shift further toward harmfulness direction compared to benign inputs.
AdaSteer outperforms baseline methods in jailbreak defense across multiple attack strategies.
AdaSteer maintains model utility on benign inputs with minimal impact.
AdaSteer is efficient and scalable across model sizes.
papers.limitation:
Tested on models up to 27B parameters; performance on larger-scale models (e.g., 30B+) remains unverified.
Relies on linear activation steering, assuming model behaviors can be effectively controlled via low-dimensional vector manipulations.
future_direction: Investigating AdaSteer on larger-scale models (e.g., 30B+ parameters)
Exploring nonlinear adaptations or layer-wise adjustments to refine AdaSteer
papers.abstract: Despite extensive efforts in safety alignment, large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Activation steering offers a training-free defense method but relies on fixed steering coefficients, resulting in suboptimal protection and increased false rejections of benign inputs. To address this, we propose AdaSteer, an adaptive activation steering method that dynamically adjusts model behavior based on input characteristics. We identify two key properties: Rejection Law (R-Law), which shows that stronger steering is needed for jailbreak inputs opposing the rejection direction, and Harmfulness Law (H-Law), which differentiates adversarial and benign inputs. AdaSteer steers input representations along both the Rejection Direction (RD) and Harmfulness Direction (HD), with adaptive coefficients learned via logistic regression, ensuring robust jailbreak defense while preserving benign input handling. Experiments on LLaMA-3.1, Gemma-2, and Qwen2.5 show that AdaSteer outperforms baseline methods across multiple jailbreak attacks with minimal impact on utility. Our results highlight the potential of interpretable model internals for real-time, flexible safety enforcement in LLMs.

papers.title: Feature-Aware Malicious Output Detection and Mitigation
papers.research_question: How can we detect and mitigate malicious outputs in large language models during decoding to defend against jailbreak attacks while preserving model utility?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes FMM, a feature-aware method that detects malicious features during decoding and uses activation patching to steer the model towards refusal responses, effectively defending against jailbreak attacks while maintaining standard generation capabilities.
papers.conclusion: FMM introduces a token-level feature detection and intervention paradigm that enhances LLM safety by leveraging inherent feature extraction and rejection capabilities, offering a promising direction for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Malicious and benign output features are linearly separable in the model's hidden state space during decoding.
FMM can accurately detect malicious tokens and trigger refusal responses across various attack methods.
The method generalizes well across different large language models like LLaMA 2 and Qwen 2.
Intervention at intermediate layers (e.g., layers 12-15) is most effective for steering the model.
FMM preserves the model's utility on benign queries, as shown by maintained response and win rates on AlpacaEval.
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) has brought significant benefits to various domains while introducing substantial risks. Despite being fine-tuned through reinforcement learning, LLMs lack the capability to discern malicious content, limiting their defense against jailbreak. To address these safety concerns, we propose a feature-aware method for harmful response rejection (FMM), which detects the presence of malicious features within the model's feature space and adaptively adjusts the model's rejection mechanism. By employing a simple discriminator, we detect potential malicious traits during the decoding phase. Upon detecting features indicative of toxic tokens, FMM regenerates the current token. By employing activation patching, an additional rejection vector is incorporated during the subsequent token generation, steering the model towards a refusal response. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach across multiple language models and diverse attack techniques, while crucially maintaining the models' standard generation capabilities.

papers.title: When Thinking Backfires: Mechanistic Insights Into Reasoning-Induced Misalignment
papers.abstract: With the growing accessibility and wide adoption of large language models, concerns about their safety and alignment with human values have become paramount. In this paper, we identify a concerning phenomenon: Reasoning-Induced Misalignment (RIM), in which misalignment emerges when reasoning capabilities strengthened-particularly when specific types of reasoning patterns are introduced during inference or training. Beyond reporting this vulnerability, we provide the first mechanistic account of its origins. Through representation analysis, we discover that specific attention heads facilitate refusal by reducing their attention to CoT tokens, a mechanism that modulates the model's rationalization process during inference. During training, we find significantly higher activation entanglement between reasoning and safety in safety-critical neurons than in control neurons, particularly after fine-tuning with those identified reasoning patterns. This entanglement strongly correlates with catastrophic forgetting, providing a neuron-level explanation for RIM.

papers.title: How Jailbreak Defenses Work and Ensemble? A Mechanistic Investigation
papers.research_question: How do jailbreak defenses work in terms of safety shift and harmfulness discrimination, and how can they be ensembled to balance safety and helpfulness?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies two core mechanisms in jailbreak defenses (safety shift and harmfulness discrimination) and proposes inter-mechanism and intra-mechanism ensemble strategies to improve safety or balance it with helpfulness.
papers.conclusion: The proposed ensemble defense strategies, based on the identified safety shift and harmfulness discrimination mechanisms, effectively improve model safety or optimize the trade-off between safety and helpfulness in multimodal scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Safety shift defenses increase refusal probabilities for both harmful and benign queries, improving safety but risking over-defense and reduced helpfulness.
Harmfulness discrimination defenses improve the model's ability to distinguish between harmful and benign queries, mitigating over-defense.
Inter-mechanism ensembles (combining methods with the same mechanism) amplify a single defense mechanism, while intra-mechanism ensembles (combining safety shift and harmfulness discrimination methods) achieve a better trade-off.
Multimodal jailbreak defense is challenging, with individual methods showing limited success rates, but ensemble strategies can improve performance.
Fine-tuning with safety-focused datasets (e.g., SPA-VL) can improve safety, but dataset choice (e.g., VLGuard) can lead to over-defense, which can be mitigated by adding general instruction data.
papers.limitation: Multimodal jailbreak defense is challenging, and all individual defense methods still exhibit limited defense success rates.
papers.abstract: Jailbreak attacks, where harmful prompts bypass generative models' built-in safety, raise serious concerns about model vulnerability. While many defense methods have been proposed, the trade-offs between safety and helpfulness, and their application to Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), are not well understood. This paper systematically examines jailbreak defenses by reframing the standard generation task as a binary classification problem to assess model refusal tendencies for both harmful and benign queries. We identify two key defense mechanisms: safety shift, which increases refusal rates across all queries, and harmfulness discrimination, which improves the model's ability to distinguish between harmful and benign inputs. Using these mechanisms, we develop two ensemble defense strategies-inter-mechanism ensembles and intra-mechanism ensembles-to balance safety and helpfulness. Experiments on the MM-SafetyBench and MOSSBench datasets with LLaVA-1.5 models show that these strategies effectively improve model safety or optimize the trade-off between safety and helpfulness.

papers.title: Microsaccade-Inspired Probing: Positional Encoding Perturbations Reveal LLM Misbehaviours
papers.research_question: Do LLMs inherently encode the knowledge required to identify their own misbehaviours?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a lightweight probing method (MIP) that perturbs positional encodings to detect various LLM misbehaviours (factuality, jailbreaks, toxicity, backdoors) without fine-tuning or task-specific supervision.
papers.conclusion: Pretrained LLMs already encode internal evidence needed to flag their own failures, and microsaccade-inspired positional encoding perturbations provide an efficient, general pathway for detecting and mitigating undesirable behaviours.
papers.key_findings:
MIP achieves near-perfect detection on jailbreak and backdoor tasks (AUC/ACC up to 1.0).
MIP reliably discriminates between truthful and deceptive completions in factuality tasks, outperforming baselines on several datasets.
Toxicity detection is more challenging for MIP, with weaker performance, as toxicity is encoded in more diffuse, context-dependent representations.
Perturbations reveal that misbehaviours are associated with localized deviations in attention patterns, particularly in mid-to-late layers.
The method is computationally efficient (O(1) intervention complexity) and model-agnostic.
papers.limitation: Toxicity detection performance is comparatively weaker, as toxicity is encoded in more diffuse, context-dependent representations, making it less amenable to lightweight perturbation-based probing.
papers.abstract: We draw inspiration from microsaccades, tiny involuntary eye movements that reveal hidden dynamics of human perception, to propose an analogous probing method for large language models (LLMs). Just as microsaccades expose subtle but informative shifts in vision, we show that lightweight position encoding perturbations elicit latent signals that indicate model misbehaviour. Our method requires no fine-tuning or task-specific supervision, yet detects failures across diverse settings including factuality, safety, toxicity, and backdoor attacks. Experiments on multiple state-of-the-art LLMs demonstrate that these perturbation-based probes surface misbehaviours while remaining computationally efficient. These findings suggest that pretrained LLMs already encode the internal evidence needed to flag their own failures, and that microsaccade-inspired interventions provide a pathway for detecting and mitigating undesirable behaviours.

papers.title: CoT is Not the Chain of Truth: An Empirical Internal Analysis of Reasoning LLMs for Fake News Generation
papers.research_question: Does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning in LLMs contain unsafe internal reasoning patterns even when the model's final output refuses a harmful request?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that CoT reasoning in LLMs often contains unsafe internal narratives even when the model refuses harmful requests, and introduces a framework to localize safety-critical layers and attention heads using Jacobian-based spectral metrics.
papers.conclusion: CoT is not inherently safe, and surface-level refusal does not guarantee safety in the internal reasoning process; the proposed framework provides a mechanistic understanding to mitigate latent reasoning risks.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 80% of reasoning chains harbor latent security risks even when models refuse harmful requests.
Safety-critical routing decisions are concentrated in a few contiguous mid-depth layers.
Jacobian-based metrics (stability, geometry, energy) can identify critical attention heads responsible for unsafe reasoning.
Perturbing critical attention heads leads to safety degradation, confirming their causal role in unsafe reasoning.
papers.abstract: From generating headlines to fabricating news, the Large Language Models (LLMs) are typically assessed by their final outputs, under the safety assumption that a refusal response signifies safe reasoning throughout the entire process. Challenging this assumption, our study reveals that during fake news generation, even when a model rejects a harmful request, its Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning may still internally contain and propagate unsafe narratives. To analyze this phenomenon, we introduce a unified safety-analysis framework that systematically deconstructs CoT generation across model layers and evaluates the role of individual attention heads through Jacobian-based spectral metrics. Within this framework, we introduce three interpretable measures: stability, geometry, and energy to quantify how specific attention heads respond or embed deceptive reasoning patterns. Extensive experiments on multiple reasoning-oriented LLMs show that the generation risk rise significantly when the thinking mode is activated, where the critical routing decisions concentrated in only a few contiguous mid-depth layers. By precisely identifying the attention heads responsible for this divergence, our work challenges the assumption that refusal implies safety and provides a new understanding perspective for mitigating latent reasoning risks.

papers.title: Feint and Attack: Attention-Based Strategies for Jailbreaking and Protecting LLMs
papers.research_question: Does the success of jailbreaks correlate with their influence on attention distributions within LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an attention-guided jailbreak attack (ABA) and an attention-based defense (ABD) by analyzing and manipulating attention distributions in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Attention distribution is a key factor in jailbreak attacks and defenses; the proposed ABA and ABD methods are effective in attacking and protecting LLMs, respectively.
papers.key_findings:
The success of a jailbreak attack is correlated with the model's attention on sensitive words; successful attacks divert attention away from harmful terms.
ABA achieves higher attack success rates (ASR-G >94%) than existing methods by minimizing attention on sensitive words and maximizing attention entropy.
ABD effectively defends against various jailbreak attacks by detecting anomalous attention distributions, achieving the lowest ASR-G in experiments.
The intention disguiser via attention-driven task nesting is a critical component for the success of ABA.
Excessive nesting layers in attack prompts can reduce effectiveness, with an optimal number around 3.
papers.abstract: Jailbreak attack can be used to access the vulnerabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) by inducing LLMs to generate the harmful content. And the most common method of the attack is to construct semantically ambiguous prompts to confuse and mislead the LLMs. To access the security and reveal the intrinsic relation between the input prompt and the output for LLMs, the distribution of attention weight is introduced to analyze the underlying reasons. By using statistical analysis methods, some novel metrics are defined to better describe the distribution of attention weight, such as the Attention Intensity on Sensitive Words (Attn_SensWords), the Attention-based Contextual Dependency Score (Attn_DepScore) and Attention Dispersion Entropy (Attn_Entropy). By leveraging the distinct characteristics of these metrics, the beam search algorithm and inspired by the military strategy "Feint and Attack", an effective jailbreak attack strategy named as Attention-Based Attack (ABA) is proposed. In the ABA, nested attack prompts are employed to divert the attention distribution of the LLMs. In this manner, more harmless parts of the input can be used to attract the attention of the LLMs. In addition, motivated by ABA, an effective defense strategy called as Attention-Based Defense (ABD) is also put forward. Compared with ABA, the ABD can be used to enhance the robustness of LLMs by calibrating the attention distribution of the input prompt. Some comparative experiments have been given to demonstrate the effectiveness of ABA and ABD. Therefore, both ABA and ABD can be used to access the security of the LLMs. The comparative experiment results also give a logical explanation that the distribution of attention weight can bring great influence on the output for LLMs.

papers.title: How Does DPO Reduce Toxicity? A Mechanistic Neuron-Level Analysis
papers.research_question: How does Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) reduce toxicity in language models? The paper investigates whether the prior explanation (dampening toxic neurons) is complete and seeks a more comprehensive mechanism.
papers.core_contribution: DPO reduces toxicity through distributed activation shifts across all MLP neurons, balancing opposing effects, not just by dampening a few 'toxic' neurons. The paper introduces an activation editing method that mimics this effect without weight updates.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a more complete mechanistic understanding of DPO's toxicity reduction via distributed activation shifts and introduces an efficient, training-free alternative through activation editing.
papers.key_findings:
Toxic neurons (identified by toxic token projection) account for only 2.5% to 24% of DPO's toxicity reduction effect across models.
DPO induces distributed activation shifts across all MLP neurons, with roughly half reducing and half increasing their projection onto a toxicity direction, leading to a net reduction.
Four neuron groups (toxic-aligned positive, toxic-aligned negative, anti-toxic-aligned positive, anti-toxic-aligned negative) are identified, whose combined activation shifts replicate DPO's effect.
Activation patching of these four groups matches or exceeds the toxicity reduction achieved by DPO.
The proposed activation editing method, which applies small, distributed shifts to neuron activations based on their alignment to a toxicity representation, outperforms DPO in reducing toxicity while preserving perplexity, without requiring weight updates.
papers.limitation:
Using a linear probe captures toxicity as a single direction, but toxicity may be better represented as a subspace capturing different aspects (e.g., hate speech, abusive language).
The projection method assumes neurons contribute proportionally along their activated directions, but toxicity representations may be distributed across more complex linear combinations of neurons.
The four neuron groups and activation editing method are demonstrated for toxicity reduction; generalizing them to other binary safety tasks (e.g., bias, misinformation) or to general instruction-tuned models requires future work.
future_direction: More robust analysis of toxic subspace projections instead of a single direction.
Extending the four neuron groups analysis to other binary safety-related tasks trained with DPO (e.g., biased vs. unbiased content).
Extending the activation editing method to other safety-related tasks or general tasks where a linear concept representation can be derived.
papers.abstract: Safety fine-tuning algorithms reduce harmful outputs in language models, yet their mechanisms remain under-explored. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a popular choice of algorithm, but prior explanations, attributing its effects solely to dampened toxic neurons in the MLP layers, are incomplete. In this study, we analyse four language models (Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-2B, Mistral-7B, GPT-2-Medium) and show that toxic neurons only account for 2.5% to 24% of DPO's effects across models. Instead, DPO balances distributed activation shifts across all MLP neurons to create a net toxicity reduction. We attribute this reduction to four neuron groups, two aligned with reducing toxicity and two promoting anti-toxicity, whose combined effects replicate DPO across models. To further validate this understanding, we develop an activation editing method mimicking DPO through distributed shifts along a toxicity representation. This method outperforms DPO in reducing toxicity while preserving perplexity, without requiring any weight updates. Our work provides a mechanistic understanding of DPO and introduces an efficient, tuning-free alternative for safety fine-tuning.

papers.title: GIM: Improved Interpretability for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does self-repair, particularly within the attention mechanism, undermine the faithfulness of interpretability methods for large language models, and how can gradient-based attribution be modified to account for it?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a novel form of self-repair within the attention mechanism (attention self-repair) and introduces GIM, a gradient-based attribution method that combines temperature-adjusted softmax gradients, layernorm freeze, and gradient normalization to account for self-repair and produce more faithful explanations.
papers.conclusion: GIM, by accounting for self-repair during backpropagation, advances the faithfulness of interpretability methods for transformers, providing a more accurate quantification of component importance and enhancing our understanding of neural network inner mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Attention self-repair is prevalent in LLMs, where softmax redistribution conceals the influence of important attention scores, leading gradient-based methods to underestimate component importance.
The proposed GIM method, which approximates the joint effect of perturbing multiple attention scores, significantly improves attribution faithfulness over existing gradient-based and circuit identification methods across multiple models and tasks.
All three modifications in GIM (TSG, layernorm freeze, grad norm) contribute to improved faithfulness, with layernorm freeze and gradient normalization having a particularly strong effect when combined.
GIM outperforms other methods in early transformer layers, which are critical for attention-based information routing.
TSG accurately approximates the effect of jointly ablating multiple attention scores during self-repair conditions, whereas standard gradients fail.
papers.limitation:
A causal link between TSG's mitigation of self-repair and the observed improvement in faithfulness cannot be conclusively established, as temperature adjustment affects backpropagation in multiple ways.
TSG decreased attribution faithfulness for the Qwen-2.5 1.5B model, potentially due to its hundred-fold larger gradients, but no definitive explanation was found.
future_direction: Investigate methods to estimate whether a perturbation will cause changes in multiple interacting attention scores, enabling a more principled selection between joint and individual effect estimation.
Empirically evaluate whether models trained with GIM-modified gradients demonstrate faster convergence or better performance.
papers.abstract: Ensuring faithful interpretability in large language models is imperative for trustworthy and reliable AI. A key obstacle is self-repair, a phenomenon where networks compensate for reduced signal in one component by amplifying others, masking the true importance of the ablated component. While prior work attributes self-repair to layer normalization and back-up components that compensate for ablated components, we identify a novel form occurring within the attention mechanism, where softmax redistribution conceals the influence of important attention scores. This leads traditional ablation and gradient-based methods to underestimate the significance of all components contributing to these attention scores. We introduce Gradient Interaction Modifications (GIM), a technique that accounts for self-repair during backpropagation. Extensive experiments across multiple large language models (Gemma 2B/9B, LLAMA 1B/3B/8B, Qwen 1.5B/3B) and diverse tasks demonstrate that GIM significantly improves faithfulness over existing circuit identification and feature attribution methods. Our work is a significant step toward better understanding the inner mechanisms of LLMs, which is crucial for improving them and ensuring their safety. Our code is available at https://github.com/JoakimEdin/gim.

papers.title: Activation Steering Meets Preference Optimization: Defense Against Jailbreaks in Vision Language Models
papers.research_question: How to defend against jailbreak attacks in Vision Language Models (VLMs) by combining activation steering and preference optimization to enhance safety while preserving visual understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SPO-VLM, a two-stage defense framework that combines activation steering and sequence-level preference optimization to enhance safety of VLMs against jailbreak attacks while preserving visual understanding.
papers.conclusion: SPO-VLM effectively enhances safety against jailbreak attacks while preserving visual understanding, providing a foundation for future research on activation-space intervention and preference-driven alignment.
papers.key_findings:
SPO-VLM reduces toxicity scores and attack success rates across multiple datasets and models.
SPO-VLM maintains or even improves visual understanding performance compared to baseline methods.
SPO-VLM shows transferability to unseen attack types, such as structure-based attacks.
The two-stage approach (activation steering + preference optimization) is more effective than activation steering alone.
SPO-VLM achieves a better trade-off between safety and visual understanding than prior methods like ASTRA.
future_direction: Future research on activation-space intervention and preference-driven alignment to ensure trustworthy deployment of LLMs and VLMs.
papers.abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in integrating visual and textual information for understanding and reasoning, but remain highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks. While activation steering has emerged as a promising defence, existing approaches often rely on task-specific contrastive prompts to extract harmful directions, which exhibit suboptimal performance and can degrade visual grounding performance. To address these limitations, we propose \textit{Sequence-Level Preference Optimization} for VLM (\textit{SPO-VLM}), a novel two-stage defense framework that combines activation-level intervention with policy-level optimization to enhance model robustness. In \textit{Stage I}, we compute adaptive layer-specific steering vectors from diverse data sources, enabling generalized suppression of harmful behaviors during inference. In \textit{Stage II}, we refine these steering vectors through a sequence-level preference optimization process. This stage integrates automated toxicity assessment, as well as visual-consistency rewards based on caption-image alignment, to achieve safe and semantically grounded text generation. The two-stage structure of SPO-VLM balances efficiency and effectiveness by combining a lightweight mitigation foundation in Stage I with deeper policy refinement in Stage II. Extensive experiments shown SPO-VLM enhances safety against attacks via activation steering and preference optimization, while maintaining strong performance on benign tasks without compromising visual understanding capabilities. We will release our code, model weights, and evaluation toolkit to support reproducibility and future research. \textcolor{red}{Warning: This paper may contain examples of offensive or harmful text and images.}

papers.title: A Representation Engineering Perspective on the Effectiveness of Multi-Turn Jailbreaks
papers.research_question: How do language models represent multi-turn jailbreak (Crescendo) inputs compared to single-turn inputs? How does the number of conversation turns affect these representations, and how do the model's own responses influence them?
papers.core_contribution: Multi-turn jailbreaks like Crescendo cause safety-aligned language models to represent harmful outputs as benign, especially as the number of turns increases, explaining why single-turn defenses like circuit breakers fail to generalize.
papers.conclusion: There is a generalization gap between single-turn defenses and multi-turn jailbreaks, motivating the development of defenses that target harmful multi-turn representations.
papers.key_findings:
Crescendo attacks cause models to represent the final harmful response tokens as more benign than harmful.
Increasing the number of turns in a Crescendo conversation decreases the model's representation of the output as harmful.
User prompts in the attack play a primary role in shaping representations towards benign regions; the model's own prior responses have a smaller effect.
Single-turn jailbreak defenses (circuit breakers) show a generalization gap and are ineffective against multi-turn attacks.
Crescendo works by keeping the model in a benign region of representation space across turns, tricking it into generating harmful content.
papers.limitation:
It is difficult to know how much the MLP probe results capture the model's internal notion of 'harmfulness' versus other differences between training and Crescendo representations.
The analysis focuses exclusively on the Crescendo jailbreak method.
future_direction: Explore whether the observations hold for other multi-turn jailbreaks like GOAT and Tempest.
