Reflecting the hypothesis, we propose ARREST (Adversarial Resilient Regulation Enhancing Safety and Truth), a unified framework that identifies and corrects drifted features, engaging both soft and hard refusals in addition to factual corrections. Our empirical results show that ARREST not only regulates misalignment but is also more versatile compared to the RLHF-aligned models in generating soft refusals due to adversarial training. We make our codebase available at https://github.com/sharanya-dasgupta001/ARREST.

papers.title: Refusal Falls off a Cliff: How Safety Alignment Fails in Reasoning?
papers.research_question: What mechanism makes the safety alignment vulnerable in reasoning models?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies the 'refusal cliff' failure mode in reasoning models, causally links it to a sparse set of 'Refusal Suppression Heads', and introduces a data selection method (Cliff-as-a-Judge) that efficiently repairs safety alignment using minimal data.
papers.conclusion: The work identifies and mechanistically characterizes the refusal cliff safety failure, links it to specific attention heads, and proposes an efficient data selection method for safety alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Many poorly-aligned reasoning models correctly identify harmful prompts and maintain strong refusal intentions during thinking, but experience a sharp drop (refusal cliff) at the final tokens before output generation.
A sparse set of attention heads (Refusal Suppression Heads) causally contribute to the refusal cliff by suppressing refusal-related representations.
Ablating just 3% of these heads can reduce attack success rates below 10%.
The proposed Cliff-as-a-Judge data selection method, which selects examples with the largest refusal cliff, achieves comparable safety improvements using only 1.7% of the vanilla safety training data.
The refusal cliff is localized to final tokens, amplified in deeper layers, preceded by a plateau, and depends on the model's thinking process.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic analysis focuses primarily on attention heads, leaving other architectural components such as MLP blocks, positional encodings, and cross-layer interactions underexplored.
The data selection method depends on having access to the model's internal representations and refusal scores, which may be impractical for proprietary systems.
future_direction: Investigation of proxy metrics or black-box analogues for the data selection method.
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) with multi-step reasoning capabilities have shown remarkable problem-solving abilities, yet they exhibit concerning safety vulnerabilities that remain poorly understood. In this work, we investigate why safety alignment fails in reasoning models through a mechanistic interpretability lens. Using a linear probing approach to trace refusal intentions across token positions, we discover a striking phenomenon termed as \textbf{refusal cliff}: many poorly-aligned reasoning models correctly identify harmful prompts and maintain strong refusal intentions during their thinking process, but experience a sharp drop in refusal scores at the final tokens before output generation. This suggests that these models are not inherently unsafe; rather, their refusal intentions are systematically suppressed. Through causal intervention analysis, we identify a sparse set of attention heads that negatively contribute to refusal behavior. Ablating just 3\% of these heads can reduce attack success rates below 10\%. Building on these mechanistic insights, we propose \textbf{Cliff-as-a-Judge}, a novel data selection method that identifies training examples exhibiting the largest refusal cliff to efficiently repair reasoning models' safety alignment. This approach achieves comparable safety improvements using only 1.7\% of the vanilla safety training data, demonstrating a less-is-more effect in safety alignment.

papers.title: Robust LLM safeguarding via refusal feature adversarial training
papers.research_question: How do adversarial attacks jailbreak LLMs, and can we design an efficient adversarial training method based on the mechanism of refusal feature ablation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that adversarial attacks jailbreak LLMs by ablating a refusal feature in the residual stream, and proposes ReFAT, an efficient adversarial training method that simulates attacks via refusal feature ablation to improve robustness.
papers.conclusion: The paper uncovers that adversarial attacks jailbreak LLMs by ablating refusal features, and proposes ReFAT, an efficient adversarial training method that improves robustness while preserving utility.
papers.key_findings:
Adversarial attacks jailbreak LLMs by ablating a refusal feature in the residual stream, as shown by high cosine similarity between attack-induced shifts and the refusal feature direction.
Refusal feature ablation approximates the worst-case adversarial perturbation that minimizes model safety score.
ReFAT, which ablates refusal features during training, improves LLM robustness against a wide range of adversarial attacks (GCG, PAIR, AutoDAN, HumanJailbreaks).
ReFAT achieves comparable or better robustness than existing adversarial training methods with significantly lower computational cost.
ReFAT preserves general model utility, as measured by MMLU and MT-Bench, and does not cause excessive over-refusals.
papers.limitation: ReFAT may not defend against attacks that use linguistic contexts very different from the harmless instructions used to compute refusal features, such as multilingual attacks or under-represented English vernacular.
future_direction: Use a more diverse set of instructions to compute refusal features to improve robustness against multilingual and varied linguistic attacks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are vulnerable to adversarial attacks that can elicit harmful responses. Defending against such attacks remains challenging due to the opacity of jailbreaking mechanisms and the high computational cost of training LLMs robustly. We demonstrate that adversarial attacks share a universal mechanism for circumventing LLM safeguards that works by ablating a dimension in the residual stream embedding space called the refusal feature. We further show that the operation of refusal feature ablation (RFA) approximates the worst-case perturbation of offsetting model safety. Based on these findings, we propose Refusal Feature Adversarial Training (ReFAT), a novel algorithm that efficiently performs LLM adversarial training by simulating the effect of input-level attacks via RFA. Experiment results show that ReFAT significantly improves the robustness of three popular LLMs against a wide range of adversarial attacks, with considerably less computational overhead compared to existing adversarial training methods.

papers.title: SafeConstellations: Steering LLM Safety to Reduce Over-Refusals Through Task-Specific Trajectory
papers.research_question: What internal representation patterns are constant for refusal and non-refusal cases in LLMs, and whether conditional steering can reduce over-refusals on benign inputs.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafeConstellations, an inference-time trajectory-shifting method that reduces over-refusal by tracking task-specific representation patterns and steering representations toward non-refusal pathways, achieving up to 73% reduction in over-refusal with minimal utility loss.
papers.conclusion: Task-specific internal trajectory patterns can be leveraged to selectively steer model behavior, reducing over-refusals while preserving appropriate safety refusals.
papers.key_findings:
Over-refusal rates vary substantially across NLP tasks and models.
LLMs encode task identity in consistent internal trajectory patterns (constellations) across layers.
SafeConstellations reduces over-refusal by up to 73% with minimal impact on utility.
Task-specific steering is more effective than generic steering, and dynamic layer selection improves performance.
Steering is most effective in mid-to-late layers (e.g., layers 14-20 in LLaMA).
papers.limitation:
Requires access to model internals, limiting applicability to closed-weight systems and APIs.
Task embeddings are static and non-adaptive, requiring periodic recomputation in dynamic environments.
Task embeddings are model-specific and do not transfer to other models.
Evaluation of utility preservation is primarily based on MMLU, not measuring factuality, coherence, calibration, or robustness.
Relies on heuristic choices for confidence thresholds, layer selection, and steering intensities.
Relies on LLM-as-a-judge protocols for evaluation, which may have biases.
future_direction: Continual updating of task embeddings in dynamic environments.
Improving batching and caching strategies for batch steering.
Generalizing to fully open-ended or multi-step instructions.
Human validation and broader audits to strengthen reliability.
papers.abstract: LLMs increasingly exhibit over-refusal behavior, where safety mechanisms cause models to reject benign instructions that superficially resemble harmful content. This phenomena diminishes utility in production applications that repeatedly rely on common prompt templates or applications that frequently rely on LLMs for specific tasks (e.g. sentiment analysis, language translation). Through comprehensive evaluation, we demonstrate that LLMs still tend to refuse responses to harmful instructions when those instructions are reframed to appear as benign tasks. Our mechanistic analysis reveal that LLMs follow distinct "constellation" patterns in embedding space as representations traverse layers, with each task maintaining consistent trajectories that shift predictably between refusal and non-refusal cases. We introduce SafeConstellations, an inference-time trajectory-shifting approach that tracks task-specific trajectory patterns and guides representations toward non-refusal pathways. By selectively guiding model behavior only on tasks prone to over-refusal, and by preserving general model behavior, our method reduces over-refusal rates by up to 73% with minimal impact on utility-offering a principled approach to mitigating over-refusals.

papers.title: Jailbreak Instruction-Tuned LLMs via end-of-sentence MLP Re-weighting
papers.research_question: How does re-weighting MLP neurons in end-of-sentence inferences affect the safety mechanisms of instruction-tuned LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that MLP layers in end-of-sentence inferences are critical for safety in instruction-tuned LLMs, and introduces two white-box jailbreak methods that re-weight MLP neurons to compromise safety.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that MLP layers in end-of-sentence inferences are critical for safety in instruction-tuned LLMs, and that re-weighting these neurons can effectively jailbreak the models, providing insights for both attack and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Re-weighting MLP neurons in end-of-sentence inferences can significantly compromise the safety of instruction-tuned LLMs.
The prompt-specific jailbreak method outperforms state-of-the-art prompt-specific methods and requires less computational time.
The prompt-general jailbreak method is comparable to state-of-the-art approaches and has minimal impact on the model's original capabilities (except for very small models).
The safety mechanism of instruction-tuned LLMs heavily relies on MLP layers in end-of-sentence inferences.
The method can also serve as a mechanism interpretability tool to identify MLP neurons strongly correlated with safety.
papers.limitation:
The method is heuristic-driven, making it more of a validation experiment rather than an optimal solution.
The precise role MLP layers play in the safety mechanism and how they impact subsequent generation processes remain open questions.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the safety mechanisms of instruction fine-tuned large language models (LLMs). We discover that re-weighting MLP neurons can significantly compromise a model's safety, especially for MLPs in end-of-sentence inferences. We hypothesize that LLMs evaluate the harmfulness of prompts during end-of-sentence inferences, and MLP layers plays a critical role in this process. Based on this hypothesis, we develop 2 novel white-box jailbreak methods: a prompt-specific method and a prompt-general method. The prompt-specific method targets individual prompts and optimizes the attack on the fly, while the prompt-general method is pre-trained offline and can generalize to unseen harmful prompts. Our methods demonstrate robust performance across 7 popular open-source LLMs, size ranging from 2B to 72B. Furthermore, our study provides insights into vulnerabilities of instruction-tuned LLM's safety and deepens the understanding of the internal mechanisms of LLMs.

papers.title: LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately
papers.research_question: Do LLMs encode harmfulness and refusal as separate concepts internally, and how can this separation be analyzed?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode harmfulness and refusal separately in their internal representations, and the harmfulness direction extracted at the instruction token can be used to manipulate and analyze model safety.
papers.conclusion: LLMs encode harmfulness and refusal separately, providing a new dimension for understanding and improving AI safety mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Harmfulness is encoded at the last token of the user instruction (t_inst), while refusal is encoded at the last token of the post-instruction tokens (t_post-inst).
Steering along the harmfulness direction can cause LLMs to reinterpret harmless inputs as harmful, while steering along the refusal direction only reinforces refusal behavior without changing harmfulness judgment.
Jailbreak methods often work by suppressing refusal signals without altering the model's internal belief that the instruction is harmful.
Harmfulness representations are fine-grained and vary across risk categories, whereas refusal directions are similar across categories.
The latent harmfulness representation can be used to build an intrinsic safeguard (Latent Guard) that performs comparably to finetuned safety models.
papers.limitation:
The study does not investigate the role of different layers in formulating refusal and harmfulness.
Experiments are limited to 7B and 8B models, so findings may not generalize to larger models.
future_direction: Study the role of each layer in harmfulness and refusal representations.
Investigate how harmfulness and refusal encoding changes with model size.
Use circuit analysis to understand the relation between internal harmfulness belief and external refusal behavior.
papers.abstract: LLMs are trained to refuse harmful instructions, but do they truly understand harmfulness beyond just refusing? Prior work has shown that LLMs' refusal behaviors can be mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, i.e., a refusal direction. In this work, we identify a new dimension to analyze safety mechanisms in LLMs, i.e., harmfulness, which is encoded internally as a separate concept from refusal. There exists a harmfulness direction that is distinct from the refusal direction. As causal evidence, steering along the harmfulness direction can lead LLMs to interpret harmless instructions as harmful, but steering along the refusal direction tends to elicit refusal responses directly without reversing the model's judgment on harmfulness. Furthermore, using our identified harmfulness concept, we find that certain jailbreak methods work by reducing the refusal signals without reversing the model's internal belief of harmfulness. We also find that adversarially finetuning models to accept harmful instructions has minimal impact on the model's internal belief of harmfulness. These insights lead to a practical safety application: The model's latent harmfulness representation can serve as an intrinsic safeguard (Latent Guard) for detecting unsafe inputs and reducing over-refusals that is robust to finetuning attacks. For instance, our Latent Guard achieves performance comparable to or better than Llama Guard 3 8B, a dedicated finetuned safeguard model, across different jailbreak methods. Our findings suggest that LLMs' internal understanding of harmfulness is more robust than their refusal decision to diverse input instructions, offering a new perspective to study AI safety.

papers.title: What Makes and Breaks Safety Fine-tuning? A Mechanistic Study
papers.research_question: What is the safety mechanism learned by the model via safety fine-tuning, and how are jailbreak and adversarial attacks able to bypass this mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Safety fine-tuning methods minimally transform MLP weights to project unsafe inputs into the null space, causing clustering of safe and unsafe activations; jailbreaks bypass safety by having activations similar to safe samples.
papers.conclusion: Safety fine-tuning minimally transforms MLP weights to project unsafe inputs into the null space, leading to clustering; jailbreaks bypass this by having activations similar to safe samples. This mechanistic understanding can inform more robust safety fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Safety fine-tuning leads to separate clusters of activations for safe and unsafe samples.
The transformation ∆W has its column-space aligned with the null-space of the instruction fine-tuned weights, making it orthogonal to the original weights.
∆W preferentially impacts unsafe samples, as their pre-activations have larger projection onto the row-space of ∆W.
The local Lipschitzness of the model decreases for unsafe samples after safety fine-tuning, making the model less sensitive to perturbations on unsafe inputs.
Jailbreak attacks (competing objectives, mismatched generalization, adversarial embeddings) have activations that are closer to safe samples, thus bypassing the safety mechanism.
future_direction: Using ∆W from stronger safety fine-tuning methods to improve weaker ones
Designing more robust safety fine-tuning protocols based on the mechanistic understanding
papers.abstract: Safety fine-tuning helps align Large Language Models (LLMs) with human preferences for their safe deployment. To better understand the underlying factors that make models safe via safety fine-tuning, we design a synthetic data generation framework that captures salient aspects of an unsafe input by modeling the interaction between the task the model is asked to perform (e.g., "design") versus the specific concepts the task is asked to be performed upon (e.g., a "cycle" vs. a "bomb"). Using this, we investigate three well-known safety fine-tuning methods -- supervised safety fine-tuning, direct preference optimization, and unlearning -- and provide significant evidence demonstrating that these methods minimally transform MLP weights to specifically align unsafe inputs into its weights' null space. This yields a clustering of inputs based on whether the model deems them safe or not. Correspondingly, when an adversarial input (e.g., a jailbreak) is provided, its activations are closer to safer samples, leading to the model processing such an input as if it were safe. We validate our findings, wherever possible, on real-world models -- specifically, Llama-2 7B and Llama-3 8B.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Safety Alignment: A Mechanistic Perspective from Safety Neurons
papers.research_question: How does safety alignment work in large language models from a mechanistic perspective, and can we identify specific neurons (safety neurons) responsible for safety behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies sparse safety neurons in LLMs that are causally responsible for safety behaviors, and shows that patching these neurons can restore safety performance. It also explains alignment tax by showing that safety and helpfulness share overlapping neurons but require different activation patterns.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a mechanistic understanding of safety alignment through safety neurons, demonstrating their causal role, transferability, and application in safeguards, paving the way for more robust alignment algorithms.
papers.key_findings:
Safety neurons are sparse (about 5% of neurons) and causally effective, with patching restoring over 90% of safety performance.
Safety neurons encode transferable mechanisms, effective across multiple red-teaming benchmarks without sacrificing general ability.
Safety neurons are robust to training randomness, with high overlap across different training runs.
Alignment tax arises because safety and helpfulness alignment share overlapping neurons but require different activation patterns for the same neurons.
Safety neurons can be used to build an effective safeguard that detects unsafe outputs before generation, improving model safety.
papers.limitation:
Safety neurons require activations from already aligned models; training-free methods to obtain these activations are not explored.
The alignment used (IA)3, a parameter-efficient method, while real-world models often undergo full fine-tuning; the impact of this difference is unknown.
The paper identifies which neurons affect safety but not how they exert this influence.
future_direction: Exploring training-free methods to obtain safety neuron activations.
Investigating how safety neurons exert their influence (the specific mechanisms).
Studying the evolution of safety neurons during pre-training.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel in various capabilities but pose safety risks such as generating harmful content and misinformation, even after safety alignment. In this paper, we explore the inner mechanisms of safety alignment through the lens of mechanistic interpretability, focusing on identifying and analyzing safety neurons within LLMs that are responsible for safety behaviors. We propose inference-time activation contrasting to locate these neurons and dynamic activation patching to evaluate their causal effects on model safety. Experiments on multiple prevalent LLMs demonstrate that we can consistently identify about $5\%$ safety neurons, and by only patching their activations we can restore over $90\%$ of the safety performance across various red-teaming benchmarks without influencing general ability. The finding of safety neurons also helps explain the ''alignment tax'' phenomenon by revealing that the key neurons for model safety and helpfulness significantly overlap, yet they require different activation patterns for the same neurons. Furthermore, we demonstrate an application of our findings in safeguarding LLMs by detecting unsafe outputs before generation. The source code is available at https://github.com/THU-KEG/SafetyNeuron.

papers.title: Steering Externalities: Benign Activation Steering Unintentionally Increases Jailbreak Risk for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do steering vectors learned from benign instruction data have unintended side-effects on model safety? Specifically, does benign activation steering (for utility) unintentionally increase jailbreak risk for LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies 'steering externalities', a phenomenon where benign activation steering (e.g., for compliance or JSON formatting) unintentionally erodes safety guardrails and significantly increases jailbreak vulnerability in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering for utility creates steering externalities that increase jailbreak risk; steered deployments should be red-teamed, and future work should develop safety-aware steering to preserve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Benign activation steering (STEER-COMPLIANCE, STEER-JSON) increases Attack Success Rates (ASR) for jailbreak attacks, acting as a 'force multiplier' that can boost ASR to over 80-99% on standard benchmarks.
Steering shifts the internal representations of harmful prompts towards regions associated with harmless requests, reducing the model's 'safety margin' and making refusal less likely.
The safety degradation occurs because steering biases the early-token distribution away from refusal prefixes, making the model more likely to enter a non-refusal generation trajectory.
The effect is observed across multiple models (Llama-2, Llama-3, Gemma) and is amplified by existing black-box jailbreak methods like CoP, PAIR, and TAP.
A preliminary safety-aware steering method (STEER-BIND) can partially mitigate the externality, suggesting a path for future safer steering techniques.
papers.limitation: t-SNE visualizations are qualitative projections and the 2D boundary is only an illustrative diagnostic.
future_direction: Develop safety-aware steering vectors (like STEER-BIND) that preserve robustness.
Include broader alignment evaluations (beyond safety refusal) when auditing steered models.
Routine red-teaming and regression testing of steered model configurations before deployment.
papers.abstract: Activation steering is a practical post-training model alignment technique to enhance the utility of Large Language Models (LLMs). Prior to deploying a model as a service, developers can steer a pre-trained model toward specific behavioral objectives, such as compliance or instruction adherence, without the need for retraining. This process is as simple as adding a steering vector to the model's internal representations. However, this capability unintentionally introduces critical and under-explored safety risks. We identify a phenomenon termed Steering Externalities, where steering vectors derived from entirely benign datasets-such as those enforcing strict compliance or specific output formats like JSON-inadvertently erode safety guardrails. Experiments reveal that these interventions act as a force multiplier, creating new vulnerabilities to jailbreaks and increasing attack success rates to over 80% on standard benchmarks by bypassing the initial safety alignment. Ultimately, our results expose a critical blind spot in deployment: benign activation steering systematically erodes the "safety margin," rendering models more vulnerable to black-box attacks and proving that inference-time utility improvements must be rigorously audited for unintended safety externalities.

papers.title: Adversarial Activation Patching: A Framework for Detecting and Mitigating Emergent Deception in Safety-Aligned Transformers
papers.research_question: How can adversarial activation patching be used to induce, detect, and mitigate emergent deceptive behaviors in safety-aligned transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces adversarial activation patching, a framework for inducing, detecting, and mitigating emergent deception in safety-aligned transformers through activation patching.
papers.conclusion: Adversarial activation patching provides a robust tool for uncovering and countering emergent deception, enhancing transformer safety.
papers.key_findings:
Adversarial activation patching can induce deceptive outputs in toy neural networks, increasing deception rates from 0% to 23.9%.
Mid-layers are more vulnerable to deception induction, with layer 2 showing the highest deception rate of 23.9% in simulations.
The framework allows for controlled simulation of vulnerabilities and quantification of deception rates.
Patching strength α linearly affects deception rates, peaking at α=0.8.
The method provides a way to proactively study emergent deception in safety-aligned models.
papers.limitation:
Toy simulations lack real LLM complexity
Human evaluations needed for subtlety
Biases in prompt curation could skew results
future_direction: Validate on open models (e.g., Llama-3) with datasets like TruthfulQA
Extend to multimodal settings for cross-modal deception
Explore scaling effects and temporal dynamics in larger models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) aligned for safety through techniques like reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) often exhibit emergent deceptive behaviors, where outputs appear compliant but subtly mislead or omit critical information. This paper introduces adversarial activation patching, a novel mechanistic interpretability framework that leverages activation patching as an adversarial tool to induce, detect, and mitigate such deception in transformer-based models. By sourcing activations from "deceptive" prompts and patching them into safe forward passes at specific layers, we simulate vulnerabilities and quantify deception rates. Through toy neural network simulations across multiple scenarios (e.g., 1000 trials per setup), we demonstrate that adversarial patching increases deceptive outputs to 23.9% from a 0% baseline, with layer-specific variations supporting our hypotheses. We propose six hypotheses, including transferability across models, exacerbation in multimodal settings, and scaling effects. An expanded literature review synthesizes over 20 key works in interpretability, deception, and adversarial attacks. Mitigation strategies, such as activation anomaly detection and robust fine-tuning, are detailed, alongside ethical considerations and future research directions. This work advances AI safety by highlighting patching's dual-use potential and provides a roadmap for empirical studies on large-scale models.

papers.title: Steering Language Model Refusal with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can amplifying sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that mediate refusal improve language model safety at inference time, and what are the trade-offs with general model capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: SAE-based feature steering can improve refusal rates for unsafe prompts but introduces a systematic trade-off, degrading performance on safe prompts and general capability benchmarks, indicating deep entanglement between safety-relevant features and general language abilities.
papers.conclusion: While SAE-based feature steering is a promising, flexible approach for enhancing language model safety without retraining, its practical deployment is limited by significant trade-offs with general capabilities, highlighting the need to better understand and address feature entanglement.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal-mediating features can be identified using a simple, handcrafted prompt.
Amplifying identified SAE features (e.g., Feature 22373) increases refusal rates for unsafe prompts in both single-turn and multi-turn jailbreak settings.
This safety improvement comes with increased over-refusal on safe prompts.
Feature steering causes significant regression in factual recall (MMLU, TruthfulQA) and reasoning (GSM8K) performance, even on benign content.
Performance regressions are not unique to safety features; steering a non-safety feature (Feature 216 for philosophy) also degrades capabilities, suggesting a general limitation of the steering approach.
papers.limitation:
The feature identification method is not scalable, relying on a single handcrafted prompt.
Feature steering introduces a trade-off between improved safety and degraded performance on unrelated capabilities.
future_direction: Developing better methods for identifying features that mediate target behaviors.
Understanding why features are entangled with unrelated capabilities and how to isolate them.
Exploring conditional steering approaches that activate interventions only when needed.
papers.abstract: Responsible deployment of language models requires mechanisms for refusing unsafe prompts while preserving model performance. While most approaches modify model weights through additional training, we explore an alternative: steering model activations at inference time via amplifying sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that mediate refusal. This work uncovers a fundamental tension between SAE steering-based safety improvements and general model capabilities. While feature steering successfully improves robustness against both single-turn and challenging multi-turn jailbreak attempts, we discover that this comes at a previously underexplored cost -- systematic degradation of performance across multiple benchmark tasks, even on safe inputs with no apparent connection to refusal behavior. This suggests that features mediating refusal may be more deeply entangled with general language model capabilities than previously understood. Our findings reveal important open questions about the nature of safety-relevant features in language models and the feasibility of isolating them for targeted intervention. While SAE-based steering shows promise as a flexible approach to enhancing language model safety, our results highlight the critical need to understand and address the mechanisms behind these capability tradeoffs before such techniques can be practically deployed.

papers.title: Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis
papers.research_question: How does safety alignment impact model behavior, why are safety mechanisms brittle, and can these issues be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis (SSAH) and identifies safety-critical components in LLMs, showing that freezing these components during fine-tuning preserves safety without sacrificing utility.
papers.conclusion: The atomic functional unit for safety in LLMs is at the neuron level, and safety alignment can be achieved with minimal intervention, emphasizing that safety alignment should not be complicated.
papers.key_findings:
Safety alignment teaches models to choose between fulfilling or refusing requests, akin to a binary classification task.
Only about 1.3-1.4% of model components are safety-critical (SCU).
Freezing SCUs during fine-tuning preserves safety performance.
Fine-tuning attacks convert safety-critical units to utility units, explaining brittleness.
Repurposing redundant units as an alignment budget minimizes alignment tax.
papers.limitation:
The evidence from probing experiments is necessary but not sufficient to fully capture the nuances of safety alignment.
The method is less effective on models with weaker initial safety alignment (e.g., Mistral).
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are overwhelmingly more and more integrated into various applications, ensuring they generate safe responses is a pressing need. Previous studies on alignment have largely focused on general instruction-following but have often overlooked the distinct properties of safety alignment, such as the brittleness of safety mechanisms. To bridge the gap, we propose the Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis (SSAH), which posits that safety alignment teaches an otherwise unsafe model to choose the correct reasoning direction - fulfill or refuse users' requests - interpreted as an implicit binary classification task. Through SSAH, we hypothesize that only a few essential components can establish safety guardrails in LLMs. We successfully identify four types of attribute-critical components: Safety Critical Unit (SCU), Utility Critical Unit (UCU), Complex Unit (CU), and Redundant Unit (RU). Our findings show that freezing certain safety-critical components during fine-tuning allows the model to retain its safety attributes while adapting to new tasks. Similarly, we show that leveraging redundant units in the pre-trained model as an "alignment budget" can effectively minimize the alignment tax while achieving the alignment goal. All considered, this paper concludes that the atomic functional unit for safety in LLMs is at the neuron level and underscores that safety alignment should not be complicated.

papers.title: Attention Slipping: A Mechanistic Understanding of Jailbreak Attacks and Defenses in LLMs
papers.research_question: What is the underlying mechanism (attention slipping) that enables jailbreak attacks in LLMs, and can we design a defense that directly counters this mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers the universal phenomenon of Attention Slipping during jailbreak attacks and proposes Attention Sharpening, a defense that directly mitigates it by applying temperature scaling to attention scores.
papers.conclusion: Attention slipping is a key mechanism in jailbreak attacks, and Attention Sharpening provides an effective and efficient defense by directly countering this phenomenon.
papers.key_findings:
Attention slipping, where models reduce attention to unsafe prototypes, is a universal phenomenon underlying jailbreak attacks.
Attention slipping occurs across diverse jailbreak methods including GCG, AutoDAN, and MSJ.
Existing defenses like Token Highlighter and SmoothLLM indirectly mitigate attention slipping.
The proposed Attention Sharpening defense effectively counters jailbreak attacks by sharpening attention distributions.
Attention Sharpening introduces no additional computational or memory overhead, making it efficient for deployment.
papers.limitation: There is a trade-off between safety and utility when using Attention Sharpening, as it may slightly degrade performance on benign tasks.
future_direction: Future work should focus on minimizing the trade-off between safety and utility.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more integral to society and technology, ensuring their safety becomes essential. Jailbreak attacks exploit vulnerabilities to bypass safety guardrails, posing a significant threat. However, the mechanisms enabling these attacks are not well understood. In this paper, we reveal a universal phenomenon that occurs during jailbreak attacks: Attention Slipping. During this phenomenon, the model gradually reduces the attention it allocates to unsafe requests in a user query during the attack process, ultimately causing a jailbreak. We show Attention Slipping is consistent across various jailbreak methods, including gradient-based token replacement, prompt-level template refinement, and in-context learning. Additionally, we evaluate two defenses based on query perturbation, Token Highlighter and SmoothLLM, and find they indirectly mitigate Attention Slipping, with their effectiveness positively correlated with the degree of mitigation achieved. Inspired by this finding, we propose Attention Sharpening, a new defense that directly counters Attention Slipping by sharpening the attention score distribution using temperature scaling. Experiments on four leading LLMs (Gemma2-9B-It, Llama3.1-8B-It, Qwen2.5-7B-It, Mistral-7B-It v0.2) show that our method effectively resists various jailbreak attacks while maintaining performance on benign tasks on AlpacaEval. Importantly, Attention Sharpening introduces no additional computational or memory overhead, making it an efficient and practical solution for real-world deployment.

papers.title: Jailbreaking Leaves a Trace: Understanding and Detecting Jailbreak Attacks from Internal Representations of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do internal representations of LLMs differ between jailbreak and benign prompts, and can these differences be used for detection and mitigation?
papers.core_contribution: Jailbreak prompts leave identifiable traces in internal representations; a tensor-based framework can detect and mitigate jailbreaks by bypassing susceptible layers without model fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations contain strong and consistent signals for jailbreak detection and mitigation, providing a lightweight, architecture-agnostic direction for improving LLM security.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak and benign prompts exhibit distinct layer-dependent latent signatures in internal representations.
These signatures can be uncovered using tensor decomposition and used for detection with high F1 scores.
Layer-wise susceptibility scores can identify layers that strongly encode jailbreak features.
Bypassing susceptible layers at inference time can block 78% of jailbreak attempts while preserving 94% of benign prompts.
The patterns are consistent across diverse model families (transformer and state-space models).
papers.limitation: Persona- or roleplay-based prompt injections can persist even after bypassing susceptible layers, and the fixed probability threshold for bypassing may not capture attacks that distribute influence across multiple layers.
future_direction: Extending the framework to additional attack families (e.g., GCG, PAIR) by incorporating corresponding prompt distributions during factor learning.
Adopting adaptive or cumulative susceptibility criteria for layer bypass.
papers.abstract: Jailbreaking large language models (LLMs) has emerged as a critical security challenge with the widespread deployment of conversational AI systems. Adversarial users exploit these models through carefully crafted prompts to elicit restricted or unsafe outputs, a phenomenon commonly referred to as Jailbreaking. Despite numerous proposed defense mechanisms, attackers continue to develop adaptive prompting strategies, and existing models remain vulnerable. This motivates approaches that examine the internal behavior of LLMs rather than relying solely on prompt-level defenses. In this work, we study jailbreaking from both security and interpretability perspectives by analyzing how internal representations differ between jailbreak and benign prompts. We conduct a systematic layer-wise analysis across multiple open-source models, including GPT-J, LLaMA, Mistral, and the state-space model Mamba, and identify consistent latent-space patterns associated with harmful inputs. We then propose a tensor-based latent representation framework that captures structure in hidden activations and enables lightweight jailbreak detection without model fine-tuning or auxiliary LLM-based detectors. We further demonstrate that the latent signals can be used to actively disrupt jailbreak execution at inference time. On an abliterated LLaMA-3.1-8B model, selectively bypassing high-susceptibility layers blocks 78% of jailbreak attempts while preserving benign behavior on 94% of benign prompts. This intervention operates entirely at inference time and introduces minimal overhead, providing a scalable foundation for achieving stronger coverage by incorporating additional attack distributions or more refined susceptibility thresholds. Our results provide evidence that jailbreak behavior is rooted in identifiable internal structures and suggest a complementary, architecture-agnostic direction for improving LLM security.

papers.title: Bleeding Pathways: Vanishing Discriminability in LLM Hidden States Fuels Jailbreak Attacks
papers.research_question: How can we improve the inherent immunity of conventionally aligned LLMs against existing jailbreak attacks without significantly sacrificing utility?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DEEPALIGN, a fine-tuning method that uses contrastive hidden-state steering to enhance LLM safety by amplifying the separation between harmful and benign hidden states during generation, reducing jailbreak success while preserving utility.
papers.conclusion: DEEPALIGN provides a unified, architecture-agnostic defense that significantly improves the safety-utility Pareto frontier by enabling continuous intrinsic toxicity detection and intervention during generation.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs' capacity to differentiate harmful from safe outputs deteriorates as generation progresses, reflected in diminishing separability of hidden states.
DEEPALIGN reduces attack success rates of diverse jailbreak attacks to near-zero or minimal levels across multiple LLMs.
DEEPALIGN preserves model utility and reduces over-refusal compared to baseline defenses.
The method's automated data generation diversifies safe response patterns, increasing resilience against attacks targeting limited refusal patterns.
DEEPALIGN maintains robustness against an adaptive attack derived from DrAttack.
papers.limitation: The adaptive attack presents a challenge by providing the model with a malicious yet seemingly benign response prefix, testing robustness against adversarial out-of-distribution prefixes.
papers.abstract: LLMs remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that exploit adversarial prompts to circumvent safety measures. Current safety fine-tuning approaches face two critical limitations. First, they often fail to strike a balance between security and utility, where stronger safety measures tend to over-reject harmless user requests. Second, they frequently miss malicious intent concealed within seemingly benign tasks, leaving models exposed to exploitation. Our work identifies a fundamental cause of these issues: during response generation, an LLM's capacity to differentiate harmful from safe outputs deteriorates. Experimental evidence confirms this, revealing that the separability between hidden states for safe and harmful responses diminishes as generation progresses. This weakening discrimination forces models to make compliance judgments earlier in the generation process, restricting their ability to recognize developing harmful intent and contributing to both aforementioned failures. To mitigate this vulnerability, we introduce DEEPALIGN - an inherent defense framework that enhances the safety of LLMs. By applying contrastive hidden-state steering at the midpoint of response generation, DEEPALIGN amplifies the separation between harmful and benign hidden states, enabling continuous intrinsic toxicity detection and intervention throughout the generation process. Across diverse LLMs spanning varying architectures and scales, it reduced attack success rates of nine distinct jailbreak attacks to near-zero or minimal. Crucially, it preserved model capability while reducing over-refusal. Models equipped with DEEPALIGN exhibited up to 3.5% lower error rates in rejecting challenging benign queries and maintained standard task performance with less than 1% decline. This marks a substantial advance in the safety-utility Pareto frontier.

papers.title: Mechanistic Analysis of Catastrophic Forgetting in Large Language Models During Continual Fine-tuning
papers.research_question: What are the primary mechanisms driving catastrophic forgetting in large language models during continual fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies three primary mechanisms of catastrophic forgetting in LLMs during sequential fine-tuning: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening around prior task minima.
papers.conclusion: Catastrophic forgetting in LLMs is driven by three interacting mechanisms (attention disruption, representational drift, loss landscape flattening), providing a mechanistic foundation for developing targeted continual learning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 15-23% of attention heads, particularly in lower layers, undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, driving early forgetting.
Representational drift in intermediate layers, measured by CKA similarity, decreases by 0.32 to 0.47, indicating significant geometric changes.
Gradient interference, especially in query and key projection matrices, strongly predicts forgetting severity (correlation r=0.87).
The loss landscape around previous task minima flattens substantially (maximum Hessian eigenvalue drops from 147.3 to 34.2), making recovery difficult.
These three mechanisms interact and operate at different timescales, with attention disruption early, representational drift accumulating, and landscape flattening emerging later.
papers.limitation:
Experimental design focused on task sequences with clear boundaries, not continuous adaptation to gradually shifting distributions.
Examined forgetting over relatively short task sequences (4 to 6 tasks), while practical systems may encounter hundreds of sequential tasks.
Mechanistic analysis primarily characterized average behaviors across many model instances; understanding individual variability and rare failure modes remains important.
future_direction: Developing architecture modifications that inherently resist the identified forgetting mechanisms, such as attention heads with built-in stability constraints or intermediate layers with protected representational subspaces.
Designing optimization algorithms that explicitly manage gradient interference, representational drift, and landscape geometry during fine-tuning.
Creating diagnostic tools that monitor mechanistic signatures in real-time to prevent catastrophic forgetting before it occurs.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit remarkable performance across diverse tasks through pre-training and fine-tuning paradigms. However, continual fine-tuning on sequential tasks induces catastrophic forgetting, where newly acquired knowledge interferes with previously learned capabilities. Despite widespread observations of this phenomenon, the mechanistic understanding remains limited. Here, we present a comprehensive mechanistic analysis of catastrophic forgetting in transformer-based LLMs during sequential fine-tuning. Through systematic experiments across multiple model scales (109B to 400B total parameters) and task sequences, we identify three primary mechanisms driving forgetting: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening. We demonstrate that forgetting severity correlates strongly with task similarity (Pearson r = 0.87) and gradient alignment metrics. Our analysis reveals that approximately 15 to 23 percent of attention heads undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, with lower layers showing greater susceptibility. These findings establish mechanistic foundations for developing targeted mitigation strategies in continual learning systems.

papers.title: NeuRel-Attack: Neuron Relearning for Safety Disalignment in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can safety alignment in large language models be bypassed by identifying and modifying specific neurons responsible for safety constraints?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes NeuRel-Attack, a method to identify and modify neurons responsible for safety alignment in LLMs, enabling effective disalignment with minimal fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: NeuRel-Attack effectively removes safety constraints in LLMs by targeting specific neurons, demonstrating a critical vulnerability and the need for improved defensive strategies.
papers.key_findings:
NeuRel-Attack achieves an average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 96%, outperforming existing jailbreak methods.
The method reduces trainable parameters by up to 83% compared to standard LoRA fine-tuning.
Optimal neuron similarity threshold for attack success is 0.85, balancing neuron selection and editing precision.
MemFlex-based selective fine-tuning strategy is the most effective among tested optimization methods.
The approach highlights vulnerabilities in current alignment techniques, emphasizing the need for robust defenses.
papers.limitation:
Fine-tuning modifications may be detectable through forensic analysis.
The method is computationally intensive and may not scale well to larger models.
Raises ethical risks by potentially enabling misuse to circumvent safety measures.
Assumes safety alignment is localized to specific neurons, which may not always be the case.
future_direction: Developing effective defenses against fine-tuning jailbreaks to improve LLM safety.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) is achieved through fine-tuning mechanisms that regulate neuron activations to suppress harmful content. In this work, we propose a novel approach to induce disalignment by identifying and modifying the neurons responsible for safety constraints. Our method consists of three key steps: Neuron Activation Analysis, where we examine activation patterns in response to harmful and harmless prompts to detect neurons that are critical for distinguishing between harmful and harmless inputs; Similarity-Based Neuron Identification, which systematically locates the neurons responsible for safe alignment; and Neuron Relearning for Safety Removal, where we fine-tune these selected neurons to restore the model's ability to generate previously restricted responses. Experimental results demonstrate that our method effectively removes safety constraints with minimal fine-tuning, highlighting a critical vulnerability in current alignment techniques. Our findings underscore the need for robust defenses against adversarial fine-tuning attacks on LLMs.

papers.title: Probing the Robustness of Large Language Models Safety to Latent Perturbations
papers.research_question: What is the robustness of safety alignment in large language models to latent perturbations, and can minor shifts in internal representations trigger unsafe responses?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a fundamental lack of local robustness in the latent representations of safety-aligned LLMs, introduces a probing method and attack (ASA) to exploit this, and proposes a defense (LAPT) that improves robustness without harming general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Current safety alignment methods lack local robustness in the internal representational space, and robust AI safety requires fortifying internal representations rather than just modifying input-output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Minor perturbations to hidden activations can successfully jailbreak safety-aligned LLMs, revealing shallow alignment.
The Activation Steering Attack (ASA) is an effective, lightweight jailbreak method that generalizes across models.
A gradient-based variant (ASAgrad) is even more effective by using harmful suffixes as targets.
Vulnerabilities are concentrated in specific 'fragile layers' within models.
Layer-wise Adversarial Patch Training (LAPT) can enhance alignment robustness against such latent attacks while preserving general task performance.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment is a key requirement for building reliable Artificial General Intelligence. Despite significant advances in safety alignment, we observe that minor latent shifts can still trigger unsafe responses in aligned models. We argue that this stems from the shallow nature of existing alignment methods, which focus on surface-level refusal behaviors without sufficiently altering internal representations. Consequently, small shifts in hidden activations can re-trigger harmful behaviors embedded in the latent space. To explore the robustness of safety alignment to latent perturbations, we introduce a probing method that measures the Negative Log-Likelihood of the original response generated by the model. This probe quantifies local sensitivity in the latent space, serving as a diagnostic tool for identifying vulnerable directions. Based on this signal, we construct effective jailbreak trajectories, giving rise to the Activation Steering Attack (ASA). More importantly, these insights offer a principled foundation for improving alignment robustness. To this end, we introduce Layer-wise Adversarial Patch Training~(LAPT), a fine-tuning strategy that inject controlled perturbations into hidden representations during training. Experimental results highlight that LAPT strengthen alignment robustness without compromising general capabilities. Our findings reveal fundamental flaws in current alignment paradigms and call for representation-level training strategies that move beyond surface-level behavior supervision. Codes and results are available at https://github.com/Carol-gutianle/LatentSafety.

papers.title: The Hidden Dimensions of LLM Alignment: A Multi-Dimensional Analysis of Orthogonal Safety Directions
papers.research_question: What is the multi-dimensional structure of safety-aligned behavior in LLMs, and how do orthogonal directions in the safety residual space represent distinct safety features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that safety alignment in LLMs is governed by multiple orthogonal directions in activation space, with a dominant direction for refusal and non-dominant directions for features like hypothetical narrative, and that manipulating these directions can bypass safety.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a multi-dimensional mechanistic understanding of what LLMs learn from safety fine-tuning, revealing that safety behavior is controlled by multiple orthogonal directions, which sheds new light on robust alignment research.
papers.key_findings:
The safety residual space is low-rank linear, with a dominant direction that predicts refusal behavior.
Non-dominant directions in the residual space represent interpretable features such as hypothetical narrative and role-playing.
Non-dominant directions causally influence the dominant direction and the model's refusal behavior.
Removing trigger tokens associated with non-dominant directions can bypass the learned safety alignment, revealing vulnerabilities.
Safety fine-tuning may learn spurious correlations from specific jailbreak patterns, limiting generalization.
papers.limitation:
As data complexity and model size increase, the effective rank of the residual space increases, making interpretation of directions more challenging.
The linearity assumption may not hold perfectly, as directions can flip between layers and extending directions indefinitely degrades generation quality.
future_direction: Analyzing the fine-tuning process in smaller intervals or grouping samples by domain.
Preventing models from learning spurious correlations through targeted interventions in activation space or data augmentation for balanced training.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models' safety-aligned behaviors, such as refusing harmful queries, can be represented by linear directions in activation space. Previous research modeled safety behavior with a single direction, limiting mechanistic understanding to an isolated safety feature. In this work, we discover that safety-aligned behavior is jointly controlled by multi-dimensional directions. Namely, we study the vector space of representation shifts during safety fine-tuning on Llama 3 8B for refusing jailbreaks. By studying orthogonal directions in the space, we first find that a dominant direction governs the model's refusal behavior, while multiple smaller directions represent distinct and interpretable features like hypothetical narrative and role-playing. We then measure how different directions promote or suppress the dominant direction, showing the important role of secondary directions in shaping the model's refusal representation. Finally, we demonstrate that removing certain trigger tokens in harmful queries can mitigate these directions to bypass the learned safety capability, providing new insights on understanding safety alignment vulnerability from a multi-dimensional perspective. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/BMPixel/safety-residual-space.

papers.title: AttentionDefense: Leveraging System Prompt Attention for Explainable Defense Against Novel Jailbreaks
papers.research_question: Can system-prompt attention from Small Language Models (SLMs) be used to characterize adversarial prompts for jailbreak detection?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes AttentionDefense, a method that uses system-prompt attention weights from SLMs to detect jailbreaks, offering an explainable, scalable, and generalizable defense.
papers.conclusion: AttentionDefense improves the explainability, scalability, and generalizability of jailbreak detection by leveraging system prompt attention from SLMs, demonstrating robustness against both known and novel jailbreak attacks.
papers.key_findings:
AttentionDefense (using Phi-2) achieves an F1-score of 0.86 on novel jailbreaks, outperforming text embedding-based classifiers and matching the performance of the much larger GPT-4 detector.
System prompt attention is a more robust and generalizable signal for jailbreak detection than semantic embeddings, performing equally well on known and novel jailbreaks.
Defining the jailbreak mechanism in the system prompt is more critical for high-precision detection than defining the payload.
Fine-tuned models (e.g., Phi-3.5-mini-instruct) may not be good candidates for using latent representations like attention for detection, as safety fine-tuning appears to obscure the signal.
AttentionDefense provides a cheaper alternative to LLM-based detectors, achieving comparable performance with models that are 800 times smaller in parameters.
papers.limitation:
AttentionDefense is anchored by a system prompt; if the system prompt is not well-engineered, the attention weights may not show meaningful differences between benign and malicious prompts.
Any change to the system prompt requires the training data to be regenerated and the classifier retrained.
AttentionDefense inherits constraints of the underlying SLM, such as small context windows.
future_direction: Investigating if system prompt attention can be used for other detector use cases outside of jailbreaks.
Exploring if a similar approach to AttentionDefense can be built using unsupervised learning to measure out-of-distribution detection, removing the requirement for labeled data.
papers.abstract: In the past few years, Language Models (LMs) have shown par-human capabilities in several domains. Despite their practical applications and exceeding user consumption, they are susceptible to jailbreaks when malicious input exploits the LM's weaknesses, causing it to deviate from its intended behavior. Current defensive strategies either classify the input prompt as adversarial or prevent LMs from generating harmful outputs. However, it is challenging to explain the reason behind the malicious nature of the jailbreak, which results in a wide variety of closed-box approaches. In this research, we propose and demonstrate that system-prompt attention from Small Language Models (SLMs) can be used to characterize adversarial prompts, providing a novel, explainable, and cheaper defense approach called AttentionDefense. Our research suggests that the attention mechanism is an integral component in understanding and explaining how LMs respond to malicious input that is not captured in the semantic meaning of text embeddings. The proposed AttentionDefense is evaluated against existing jailbreak benchmark datasets. Ablation studies show that SLM-based AttentionDefense has equivalent or better jailbreak detection performance compared to text embedding-based classifiers and GPT-4 zero-shot detectors.To further validate the efficacy of the proposed approach, we generate a dataset of novel jailbreak variants of the existing benchmark dataset using a closed-loop LLM-based multi-agent system. We demonstrate that the proposed AttentionDefense approach performs robustly on this novel jailbreak dataset while existing approaches suffer in performance. Additionally, for practical purposes AttentionDefense is an ideal solution as it has the computation requirements of a small LM but the performance of a LLM detector.

papers.title: SafeLLM: Unlearning Harmful Outputs from Large Language Models against Jailbreak Attacks
papers.research_question: How can we defend against jailbreak attacks on Large Language Models by unlearning harmful outputs while preserving linguistic fluency and general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafeLLM, a token-level unlearning framework that integrates dynamic detection, FFN activation tracing, and constrained optimization to suppress harmful outputs in LLMs against jailbreak attacks while preserving general performance.
papers.conclusion: SafeLLM achieves irreversible forgetting of harmful behavior, significantly reducing jailbreak attack success rates without degrading general performance, offering a scalable and proactive defense for LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
SafeLLM significantly reduces Attack Success Rates (ASR) across jailbreak benchmarks compared to baseline methods like SFT and DPO.
It maintains general performance on benign datasets such as OpenBookQA and TruthfulQA after unlearning.
SafeLLM enables irreversible forgetting of harmful behaviors by targeting FFN substructures responsible for harmful token generation.
The framework demonstrates robustness to unseen adversarial prompts through feature-driven generalization.
Ablation studies show that dynamic fusion weights and adaptive trust-region bounds optimize the safety-utility trade-off.
future_direction: Advance unlearning techniques to tackle broader challenges related to fairness, transparency, and adversarial threats in multi-modal LLMs.
papers.abstract: Jailbreak attacks pose a serious threat to the safety of Large Language Models (LLMs) by crafting adversarial prompts that bypass alignment mechanisms, causing the models to produce harmful, restricted, or biased content. In this paper, we propose SafeLLM, a novel unlearning-based defense framework that unlearn the harmful knowledge from LLMs while preserving linguistic fluency and general capabilities. SafeLLM employs a three-stage pipeline: (1) dynamic unsafe output detection using a hybrid approach that integrates external classifiers with model-internal evaluations; (2) token-level harmful content tracing through feedforward network (FFN) activations to localize harmful knowledge; and (3) constrained optimization to suppress unsafe behavior without degrading overall model quality. SafeLLM achieves targeted and irreversible forgetting by identifying and neutralizing FFN substructures responsible for harmful generation pathways. Extensive experiments on prominent LLMs (Vicuna, LLaMA, and GPT-J) across multiple jailbreak benchmarks show that SafeLLM substantially reduces attack success rates while maintaining high general-purpose performance. Compared to standard defense methods such as supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization, SafeLLM offers stronger safety guarantees, more precise control over harmful behavior, and greater robustness to unseen attacks. Moreover, SafeLLM maintains the general performance after the harmful knowledge unlearned. These results highlight unlearning as a promising direction for scalable and effective LLM safety.

papers.title: The Unintended Trade-off of AI Alignment:Balancing Hallucination Mitigation and Safety in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do truthfulness-enhancing edits affect jailbreak susceptibility, and which components mediate the truthfulness-safety interaction?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a trade-off between improving truthfulness and maintaining safety in LLMs, and proposes a method using sparse autoencoders to disentangle refusal and hallucination features, preserving the refusal subspace during fine-tuning to mitigate the trade-off.
papers.conclusion: There is a trade-off between truthfulness and refusal alignment in LLMs, and the proposed method using sparse autoencoders to disentangle features and preserve the refusal subspace during fine-tuning can maintain safety while preventing hallucinations from increasing.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness-enhancing edits (e.g., ITI, TruthX) increase jailbreak susceptibility, revealing a trade-off between factuality and safety.
Hallucination and refusal behaviors share overlapping internal representations in specific attention heads.
Fine-tuning on benign datasets can degrade safety alignment due to shared representational space between refusal and hallucination features.
The proposed SAE-guided fine-tuning method preserves refusal behavior while improving task utility, mitigating the trade-off.
papers.limitation:
Further investigation is needed to interpret how different alignment methods affect knowledge suppression and whether their impact varies across model architectures.
The analysis primarily examined specific components; a more comprehensive study of additional layers and mechanisms may yield deeper insights.
The proposed solution relies on a trained SAE, which may limit its practicality for fine-tuning at scale.
papers.abstract: Hallucination in large language models (LLMs) has been widely studied in recent years, with progress in both detection and mitigation aimed at improving truthfulness. Yet, a critical side effect remains largely overlooked: enhancing truthfulness can negatively impact safety alignment. In this paper, we investigate this trade-off and show that increasing factual accuracy often comes at the cost of weakened refusal behavior. Our analysis reveals that this arises from overlapping components in the model that simultaneously encode hallucination and refusal information, leading alignment methods to suppress factual knowledge unintentionally. We further examine how fine-tuning on benign datasets, even when curated for safety, can degrade alignment for the same reason. To address this, we propose a method that disentangles refusal-related features from hallucination features using sparse autoencoders, and preserves refusal behavior during fine-tuning through subspace orthogonalization. This approach prevents hallucinations from increasing while maintaining safety alignment.We evaluate our method on commonsense reasoning tasks and harmful benchmarks (AdvBench and StrongReject). Results demonstrate that our approach preserves refusal behavior and task utility, mitigating the trade-off between truthfulness and safety.

papers.title: LLM-VA: Resolving the Jailbreak-Overrefusal Trade-off via Vector Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we simultaneously address both jailbreak and over-refusal in safety-aligned LLMs without fine-tuning or architectural changes?
papers.core_contribution: LLM-V A aligns answer vectors with benign vectors through closed-form weight updates to resolve the jailbreak-overrefusal trade-off without fine-tuning or architectural changes.
papers.conclusion: LLM-V A effectively resolves the jailbreak-overrefusal trade-off by aligning vectors, without requiring fine-tuning or architectural changes.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode answer decisions and safety assessments as nearly orthogonal vectors.
Aligning these vectors through closed-form weight updates simultaneously reduces jailbreak and over-refusal.
LLM-V A achieves 11.45% higher F1 than the best baseline while preserving 95.92% utility.
The method automatically adapts to each model's safety bias without manual tuning.
The method is effective across 12 LLMs from 5 model families.
papers.limitation:
Binary toxicity assumption (only benign vs. toxic), whereas real-world toxicity is nuanced and multi-dimensional.
Model scale: experiments cover models up to 14B parameters; effectiveness on larger models (e.g., 70B+) remains to be validated.
Training data dependency: requires labeled benign/toxic samples for SVM training; data quality and representativeness affect performance.
Difficulty applying to LLMs with chain-of-thought reasoning due to computational expense and randomness in reasoning steps.
Model-specific tuning required for optimal iteration count and layer selection.
future_direction: Extending LLM-V A to multi-class or fine-grained toxicity classification.
Validating effectiveness on larger models (e.g., 70B+).
Improving generalization to unseen datasets.
papers.abstract: Safety-aligned LLMs suffer from two failure modes: jailbreak (answering harmful inputs) and over-refusal (declining benign queries). Existing vector steering methods adjust the magnitude of answer vectors, but this creates a fundamental trade-off -- reducing jailbreak increases over-refusal and vice versa. We identify the root cause: LLMs encode the decision to answer (answer vector $v_a$) and the judgment of input safety (benign vector $v_b$) as nearly orthogonal directions, treating them as independent processes. We propose LLM-VA, which aligns $v_a$ with $v_b$ through closed-form weight updates, making the model's willingness to answer causally dependent on its safety assessment -- without fine-tuning or architectural changes. Our method identifies vectors at each layer using SVMs, selects safety-relevant layers, and iteratively aligns vectors via minimum-norm weight modifications. Experiments on 12 LLMs demonstrate that LLM-VA achieves 11.45% higher F1 than the best baseline while preserving 95.92% utility, and automatically adapts to each model's safety bias without manual tuning. Code and models are available at https://hotbento.github.io/LLM-VA-Web/.

papers.title: Understanding and Mitigating Over-refusal for Large Language Models via Safety Representation
papers.research_question: How do over-refusal samples alter a model's perception of safety, leading to rejection responses? How can we better balance safety and over-refusal?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes over-refusal in LLMs from a representation perspective, finding that over-refusal samples reside at the boundary between benign and malicious representations, and proposes the MOSR method with overlap-aware loss weighting and context-aware augmentation to mitigate over-refusal while maintaining safety.
papers.conclusion: The paper attributes over-refusal to pseudo-malicious representations lying in the boundary region between malicious and benign samples and proposes two strategies (overlap-aware loss weighting and context-aware augmentation) that mitigate the tendency for over-refusal sample representations to migrate toward the rejection space during alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Over-refusal samples reside at the boundary between benign and malicious samples in the representation space, causing the model to misclassify them as malicious.
The proposed MOSR method, incorporating overlap-aware loss weighting and context-aware augmentation, effectively mitigates over-refusal while largely maintaining model safety.
Existing defense methods often exhibit a severe imbalance between safety and over-refusal, sacrificing utility for higher malicious prompt rejection rates.
MOSR maintains the general capabilities of the model, as evaluated on standard benchmarks like MMLU and GSM8K.
The balance between safety and over-refusal is challenging due to the high similarity between over-refusal and malicious samples in representation space.
papers.limitation:
The paper focuses on single-round scenarios; multi-round over-refusal scenarios are not addressed.
Fine-tuning large language models with the proposed method remains costly.
future_direction: Multi-turn over-refusal scenarios, including developing benchmarks for multi-round over-refusal and safety.
Exploring lower-cost mitigation approaches, such as dynamic reasoning intervention methods based on representation engineering.
papers.abstract: Large language models demonstrate powerful capabilities across various natural language processing tasks, yet they also harbor safety vulnerabilities. To enhance LLM safety, various jailbreak defense methods have been proposed to guard against harmful outputs. However, improvements in model safety often come at the cost of severe over-refusal, failing to strike a good balance between safety and usability. In this paper, we first analyze the causes of over-refusal from a representation perspective, revealing that over-refusal samples reside at the boundary between benign and malicious samples. Based on this, we propose MOSR, designed to mitigate over-refusal by intervening the safety representation of LLMs. MOSR incorporates two novel components: (1) Overlap-Aware Loss Weighting, which determines the erasure weight for malicious samples by quantifying their similarity to pseudo-malicious samples in the representation space, and (2) Context-Aware Augmentation, which supplements the necessary context for rejection decisions by adding harmful prefixes before rejection responses. Experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches in mitigating over-refusal while largely maintaining safety. Overall, we advocate that future defense methods should strike a better balance between safety and over-refusal.

papers.title: Spot Risks Before Speaking! Unraveling Safety Attention Heads in Large Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can internal activations of large vision-language models, specifically attention heads, be used to detect malicious prompts and understand inner safety mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Discovers safety attention heads in LVLMs that can detect malicious prompts and constructs an efficient, tuning-free defender (SAHs) based on these heads.
papers.conclusion: Leveraging safety attention heads effectively protects LVLMs from malicious prompts with minimal inference overhead, as confirmed by experiments across various attacks.
papers.key_findings:
Activations from attention heads can linearly separate malicious prompts from benign ones.
Sparse attention heads generate strongly discriminative features for identifying malicious inputs.
Safety heads act as specialized shields; ablating them reduces model safety without affecting utility.
The reduced number of safety heads in LVLMs increases their vulnerability compared to LLMs.
The constructed detector using safety heads shows strong zero-shot generalization capabilities.
papers.abstract: With the integration of an additional modality, large vision-language models (LVLMs) exhibit greater vulnerability to safety risks (e.g., jailbreaking) compared to their language-only predecessors. Although recent studies have devoted considerable effort to the post-hoc alignment of LVLMs, the inner safety mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we discover that internal activations of LVLMs during the first token generation can effectively identify malicious prompts across different attacks. This inherent safety perception is governed by sparse attention heads, which we term ``safety heads." Further analysis reveals that these heads act as specialized shields against malicious prompts; ablating them leads to higher attack success rates, while the model's utility remains unaffected. By locating these safety heads and concatenating their activations, we construct a straightforward but powerful malicious prompt detector that integrates seamlessly into the generation process with minimal extra inference overhead. Despite its simple structure of a logistic regression model, the detector surprisingly exhibits strong zero-shot generalization capabilities. Experiments across various prompt-based attacks confirm the effectiveness of leveraging safety heads to protect LVLMs. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/Ziwei-Zheng/SAHs}.

papers.title: Safety Alignment via Constrained Knowledge Unlearning
papers.research_question: How can we improve the safety alignment of large language models against jailbreak attacks by unlearning harmful knowledge while preserving useful knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Constrained Knowledge Unlearning (CKU), a safety alignment method that identifies and fixes knowledge-related neurons in MLP layers during unlearning to remove harmful knowledge while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: CKU effectively enhances LLM safety against jailbreak attacks by unlearning harmful knowledge while preserving general capabilities, offering a promising approach for safety alignment and knowledge editing.
papers.key_findings:
CKU achieves a superior balance between safety and utility compared to existing methods like RSFT, GAM, Eraser, Safe Unlearning, and Circuit Break.
Fixing 80% of neurons (Neuron Locking Rate=0.8) during unlearning yields the greatest safety improvement.
Unlearning applied only to a subset of MLP layers (layers 8-12) results in a fourfold increase in safety with only a 0.15% reduction in utility.
The neuron selection mechanism based on SNIP scoring is more effective than random selection for preserving utility during unlearning.
