We study the effectiveness of the Crescendo multi-turn jailbreak at the level of intermediate model representations and find that safety-aligned LMs often represent Crescendo responses as more benign than harmful, especially as the number of conversation turns increases. Our analysis indicates that at each turn, Crescendo prompts tend to keep model outputs in a "benign" region of representation space, effectively tricking the model into fulfilling harmful requests. Further, our results help explain why single-turn jailbreak defenses like circuit breakers are generally ineffective against multi-turn attacks, motivating the development of mitigations that address this generalization gap.

papers.title: Guiding Giants: Lightweight Controllers for Weighted Activation Steering in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we achieve fine-grained, adaptive inference-time control of LLM behavior for safety without altering the original model parameters?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a lightweight, trainable controller network for adaptive inference-time steering that dynamically modulates a pre-computed 'refusal direction' vector with a learned scalar magnitude and layer-specific weights, significantly improving LLM safety without altering base model parameters.
papers.conclusion: Weighted Activation Steering (WAS) is an effective, lightweight inference-time mechanism that significantly enhances LLM safety by dynamically modulating activations, offering a computationally efficient alternative to fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
WAS significantly increases refusal rates on safety benchmarks (e.g., 93% on ToxicChat for Llama-3.1-8B) while preserving performance on general capability benchmarks like AlpacaEval.
The learned layer-specific weights are essential for effective steering; using uniform weights leads to a 21.2% drop in refusal rate on ToxicChat.
The controller learns interpretable, layer-specific steering patterns that vary across different safety categories (e.g., harassment, illegal content).
WAS offers a favorable trade-off between safety performance and inference latency compared to other activation steering methods like ITI and ACT.
Steering is most effective when applied to all layers, with late layers being particularly important for refusal representations.
papers.limitation:
Ambiguous or borderline harmful prompts might not trigger a strong enough controller response, leading to undesired compliance.
The controller may not generalize to novel harm types or diverse benign interactions not covered in the training data.
The definitions of 'harm' and 'benign' are subjective and can embed biases from the training datasets.
papers.abstract: Controlling undesirable Large Language Model (LLM) behaviors, such as the generation of unsafe content or failing to adhere to safety guidelines, often relies on costly fine-tuning. Activation steering provides an alternative for inference-time control, but existing methods typically lack fine-grained, adaptive mechanisms. We introduce a novel approach using a lightweight, trainable controller network integrated during inference. This controller network observes specific intermediate LLM activations and predicts both a global scaling factor and layer-specific weights. The predicted global scaling factor and layer-specific weights then dynamically modulate the intensity of a steering patch, derived from a pre-computed "refusal direction" vector, applied across the LLM's layers during generation. Trained on activations from both harmful and benign prompts, our controller learns to discriminatively apply nuanced, layer-aware interventions, activating steering primarily for harmful inputs. Experiments using safety benchmarks like ToxicChat & In-The-Wild Jailbreak Prompts demonstrate that our weighted steering controller significantly increases refusal rates compared to the base LLM, achieving targeted behavioral modification without altering the original model parameters. Our experiments with Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-1B & Mistral-7B show our approach outperforms existing methods, presenting an efficient and adaptive method for fine-grained control over LLM behavior at inference time.

papers.title: Why Safeguarded Ships Run Aground? Aligned Large Language Models' Safety Mechanisms Tend to Be Anchored in The Template Region
papers.research_question: Why are aligned large language models vulnerable to jailbreak attacks? The paper hypothesizes that their safety mechanisms are overly reliant on the template region (Template-Anchored Safety Alignment).
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies Template-Anchored Safety Alignment (TASA) as a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, where safety mechanisms overly rely on the template region, and shows that detaching safety mechanisms from this region can mitigate jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Template-anchored safety alignment is a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, and future safety alignment techniques should reduce reliance on the template region to improve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Attention shifts from the instruction region to the template region when processing harmful inputs.
The template region has a causal effect on safety decisions, as shown by activation patching.
Intervening in the template region (TEMP PATCH) can jailbreak models with high success rates.
Jailbreak attacks suppress harmfulness features in the template region.
Harmfulness probes from the template region can be transferred to response generation to detect harmful content.
papers.limitation:
The analysis may not generalize to all safety-aligned LLMs, as some may have mitigated TASA through training data or feature suppression.
The proposed detachment method does not eliminate the learned safety shortcuts and is only a proof-of-concept.
future_direction: Develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.
Integrate adversarial defense patterns during training.
Proactively suppress shortcut-prone features during alignment.
papers.abstract: The safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) remains vulnerable, as their initial behavior can be easily jailbroken by even relatively simple attacks. Since infilling a fixed template between the input instruction and initial model output is a common practice for existing LLMs, we hypothesize that this template is a key factor behind their vulnerabilities: LLMs' safety-related decision-making overly relies on the aggregated information from the template region, which largely influences these models' safety behavior. We refer to this issue as template-anchored safety alignment. In this paper, we conduct extensive experiments and verify that template-anchored safety alignment is widespread across various aligned LLMs. Our mechanistic analyses demonstrate how it leads to models' susceptibility when encountering inference-time jailbreak attacks. Furthermore, we show that detaching safety mechanisms from the template region is promising in mitigating vulnerabilities to jailbreak attacks. We encourage future research to develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.

papers.title: HSF: Defending against Jailbreak Attacks with Hidden State Filtering
papers.research_question: How can we defend against jailbreak attacks on LLMs by leveraging their hidden state representations to preemptively identify and reject adversarial inputs before inference?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes HSF, a plug-in defense module that uses hidden states from the last decoder layer to classify and block jailbreak attacks before inference, with minimal computational overhead.
papers.conclusion: HSF effectively defends against state-of-the-art jailbreak attacks by leveraging the alignment capabilities reflected in LLM hidden states, offering an efficient and modular defense mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Aligned LLMs can naturally distinguish between harmful, benign, and jailbreak queries within their hidden state representation space.
HSF significantly reduces the Attack Success Rate (ASR) against six state-of-the-art jailbreak attacks while maintaining a low false positive rate.
HSF's defense performance is robust across different models (Llama2, Vicuna, Mistral) and requires only lightweight training of an added MLP classifier.
The method incurs negligible inference overhead and does not alter the core LLM architecture.
papers.limitation: Limited generalizability; HSF is tailored to specific LLMs and requires retraining when applied to other models.
future_direction: Explore how to leverage LLM hidden states to build more flexible harmful-behavior detectors.
Enhance jailbreak attack prevention through Retrieval-Augmented Generation methods.
papers.abstract: With the growing deployment of LLMs in daily applications like chatbots and content generation, efforts to ensure outputs align with human values and avoid harmful content have intensified. However, increasingly sophisticated jailbreak attacks threaten this alignment, aiming to induce unsafe outputs. Current defense efforts either focus on prompt rewriting or detection, which are limited in effectiveness due to the various design of jailbreak prompts, or on output control and detection, which are computationally expensive as they require LLM inference. Therefore, designing a pre-inference defense method that resists diverse jailbreak prompts is crucial for preventing LLM jailbreak attacks. We observe that jailbreak attacks, safe queries, and harmful queries exhibit different clustering patterns within the LLM's hidden state representation space. This suggests that by leveraging the LLM's hidden state representational capabilities, we can analyze the LLM's forthcoming behavior and proactively intervene for defense. In this paper, we propose a jailbreak attack defense strategy based on a Hidden State Filter (HSF), a lossless architectural defense mechanism that enables the model to preemptively identify and reject adversarial inputs before the inference process begins. We activate its defensive potential through an additional plugin module, effectively framing the defense task as a classification problem. Experimental results on two benchmark datasets, utilizing three different LLMs, show that HSF significantly enhances resilience against six cutting-edge jailbreak attacks. It significantly reduces the success rate of jailbreak attacks while minimally impacting responses to benign user queries, with negligible inference overhead, and outperforming defense baselines.Our code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Hidden-State-Filtering-8652/

papers.title: LatentGuard: Controllable Latent Steering for Robust Refusal of Attacks and Reliable Response Generation
papers.research_question: How can we achieve robust safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) with fine-grained controllability and interpretability at the representation level?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LATENTGUARD, a three-stage framework combining reasoning-enhanced fine-tuning with supervised latent space control via a structured VAE to achieve interpretable and precise safety steering in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: LATENTGUARD enables interpretable and controllable refusal in LLMs by integrating reasoning-aware fine-tuning with supervised latent space steering, achieving a favorable balance between safety enforcement and practical utility.
papers.key_findings:
LATENTGUARD significantly reduces unnecessary refusals on benign prompts (from 41% to 0%) while maintaining high refusal rates on adversarial prompts.
The method demonstrates strong performance against advanced attack strategies (Adaptive, PAP, DRA), improving refusal rates and safety scores.
Latent space intervention is most effective in middle-to-upper transformer layers (e.g., layers 13-17 for benign preservation, 15-23 for attack mitigation).
The framework generalizes across different model architectures, as validated on both Qwen3-8B and Mistral-7B.
Supervised latent disentanglement enables targeted manipulation of safety-related features (attack type, method, benign indicator) for controllable refusal behavior.
papers.limitation:
Depends on structured supervision signals (attack type, prompt category) from an auxiliary classifier; errors in this upstream model may propagate and degrade control reliability.
Focuses on MLP activations; extending to other components (e.g., attention) requires new supervision designs and may affect disentanglement.
Cross-architecture generalization of latent control remains open, especially for smaller or quantized models.
Real-time deployment demands efficient latent intervention and decoding strategies, which are deferred to future work.
future_direction: Scale the framework to larger models.
Extend it to unseen or evolving attack strategies.
Develop dynamic latent control schemes for real-time, context-sensitive safety interventions.
papers.abstract: Achieving robust safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) while preserving their utility remains a fundamental challenge. Existing approaches often struggle to balance comprehensive safety with fine-grained controllability at the representation level. We introduce LATENTGUARD, a novel three-stage framework that combines behavioral alignment with supervised latent space control for interpretable and precise safety steering. Our approach begins by fine-tuning an LLM on rationalized datasets containing both reasoning-enhanced refusal responses to adversarial prompts and reasoning-enhanced normal responses to benign queries, establishing robust behavioral priors across both safety-critical and utility-preserving scenarios. We then train a structured variational autoencoder (VAE) on intermediate MLP activations, supervised by multi-label annotations including attack types, attack methods, and benign indicators. This supervision enables the VAE to learn disentangled latent representations that capture distinct adversarial characteristics while maintaining semantic interpretability. Through targeted manipulation of learned latent dimensions, LATENTGUARD achieves selective refusal behavior, effectively blocking harmful requests while preserving helpfulness for legitimate use cases. Experiments on Qwen3-8B demonstrate significant improvements in both safety controllability and response interpretability without compromising utility. Cross-architecture validation on Mistral-7B confirms the generalizability of our latent steering approach, showing consistent effectiveness across different model families. Our results suggest that structured representation-level intervention offers a promising pathway toward building safer yet practical LLM systems.

papers.title: The Geometry of Harmfulness in LLMs through Subconcept Probing
papers.research_question: How can we understand and mitigate harmful behaviors in LLMs by decomposing harmfulness into subconcepts and analyzing their geometric structure in activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that harmfulness in LLMs can be represented as a low-rank linear subspace in activation space, and steering in the dominant direction of this subspace can effectively reduce harmful generations with minimal utility loss.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a geometric approach to understanding and mitigating harmfulness in LLMs, underscoring the value of multidimensional probing for uncovering latent harmful behaviors and designing more controllable and transparent models.
papers.key_findings:
The harmfulness subspace formed by 55 subconcept directions is low-rank linear, with a single dominant direction capturing most of the variance.
Steering in the dominant direction allows for near elimination of harmful responses on jailbreak datasets with only a minor decrease in utility.
Linear probes for harmfulness subconcepts achieve high accuracy and generalize to out-of-distribution data.
Ablating the entire harmfulness subspace or just the dominant direction reduces jailbreak penetration with minimal utility loss.
The method works on two different models (Llama and Qwen), though with some differences in effectiveness.
papers.limitation:
The study has limited model testing and may not generalize well to other untested models of differing scales.
The subcategories of harmfulness tested are not extensive and may not include all possible subcategories of harmful model responses.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have intensified the need to understand and reliably curb their harmful behaviours. We introduce a multidimensional framework for probing and steering harmful content in model internals. For each of 55 distinct harmfulness subconcepts (e.g., racial hate, employment scams, weapons), we learn a linear probe, yielding 55 interpretable directions in activation space. Collectively, these directions span a harmfulness subspace that we show is strikingly low-rank. We then test ablation of the entire subspace from model internals, as well as steering and ablation in the subspace's dominant direction. We find that dominant direction steering allows for near elimination of harmfulness with a low decrease in utility. Our findings advance the emerging view that concept subspaces provide a scalable lens on LLM behaviour and offer practical tools for the community to audit and harden future generations of language models.

papers.title: ALERT: Zero-shot LLM Jailbreak Detection via Internal Discrepancy Amplification
papers.research_question: How to detect jailbreak attacks in a zero-shot setting where no jailbreak templates are available during training, by amplifying internal feature discrepancies between benign and jailbreak prompts.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a zero-shot jailbreak detection task and a detector (ALERT) that amplifies internal discrepancies at layer, module, and token levels to identify unseen jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: ALERT demonstrates strong zero-shot detection capability against unseen jailbreak attacks, significantly outperforming existing baselines and satisfying practicality principles for real-world deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Shallow layers (particularly the 3rd and 4th) encode safety-relevant semantics and exhibit large distributional discrepancies.
Gating and context features within the FFN provide stronger zero-shot discriminative signals than hidden states due to decoupled activation responses.
Jailbreak templates exhibit a larger token-level distribution gap from benign and harmful prompts compared to harmful instructions.
ALERT consistently achieves over 90% Accuracy and F1-score in zero-shot detection, outperforming baselines by at least 10% on average.
The proposed amplification mechanisms progressively improve detection performance, with module-wise amplification yielding the largest gain.
papers.limitation: The detector adopts a relatively simple VIB-based design; more advanced designs from generalization and domain adaptation could further improve robustness.
future_direction: Incorporate techniques from generalization and domain adaptation to explicitly reduce the domain gap between harmful and jailbreak prompts.
Explore using gating and context features for jailbreak mitigation through post-training strategies like reinforcement learning.
papers.abstract: Despite rich safety alignment strategies, large language models (LLMs) remain highly susceptible to jailbreak attacks, which compromise safety guardrails and pose serious security risks. Existing detection methods mainly detect jailbreak status relying on jailbreak templates present in the training data. However, few studies address the more realistic and challenging zero-shot jailbreak detection setting, where no jailbreak templates are available during training. This setting better reflects real-world scenarios where new attacks continually emerge and evolve. To address this challenge, we propose a layer-wise, module-wise, and token-wise amplification framework that progressively magnifies internal feature discrepancies between benign and jailbreak prompts. We uncover safety-relevant layers, identify specific modules that inherently encode zero-shot discriminative signals, and localize informative safety tokens. Building upon these insights, we introduce ALERT (Amplification-based Jailbreak Detector), an efficient and effective zero-shot jailbreak detector that introduces two independent yet complementary classifiers on amplified representations. Extensive experiments on three safety benchmarks demonstrate that ALERT achieves consistently strong zero-shot detection performance. Specifically, (i) across all datasets and attack strategies, ALERT reliably ranks among the top two methods, and (ii) it outperforms the second-best baseline by at least 10% in average Accuracy and F1-score, and sometimes by up to 40%.

papers.title: Enhancing Multiple Dimensions of Trustworthiness in LLMs via Sparse Activation Control
papers.research_question: How can we enhance multiple dimensions of trustworthiness (safety, factuality, bias) in LLMs simultaneously without training, by controlling sparse activations in specific model components?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Activation Control, a training-free method that enhances multiple trustworthiness dimensions in LLMs by identifying sparse, task-specific attention heads and controlling their representations using Gaussian Mixture Models, avoiding control conflicts.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Activation Control is an effective training-free method for enhancing multi-dimensional trustworthiness in LLMs by leveraging sparse and independent task-specific components.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse Activation Control can enhance safety, factuality, and bias simultaneously without significant interference, outperforming representation engineering baselines in multi-task control.
Attention heads for different tasks are sparse and have minimal overlap, allowing independent control.
The method does not significantly harm general model performance on MMLU and CSQA.
The method generalizes to other models (Qwen series) and additional trustworthiness tasks (robustness, privacy).
Control shifts head outputs towards task-relevant tokens, as shown by unembedding projections.
papers.limitation:
Relies on construction of paired stimuli, which may require domain knowledge.
Experiments are limited to a few models and tasks.
future_direction: Extend to more tasks and models
Explore theoretical foundations of sparsity
papers.abstract: As the development and application of Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance rapidly, enhancing their trustworthiness and aligning them with human preferences has become a critical area of research. Traditional methods rely heavily on extensive data for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), but representation engineering offers a new, training-free approach. This technique leverages semantic features to control the representation of LLM's intermediate hidden states, enabling the model to meet specific requirements such as increased honesty or heightened safety awareness. However, a significant challenge arises when attempting to fulfill multiple requirements simultaneously. It proves difficult to encode various semantic contents, like honesty and safety, into a singular semantic feature, restricting its practicality. In this work, we address this issue through ``Sparse Activation Control''. By delving into the intrinsic mechanisms of LLMs, we manage to identify and pinpoint components that are closely related to specific tasks within the model, i.e., attention heads. These heads display sparse characteristics that allow for near-independent control over different tasks. Our experiments, conducted on the open-source Llama series models, have yielded encouraging results. The models were able to align with human preferences on issues of safety, factuality, and bias concurrently.

papers.title: Omni-Safety under Cross-Modality Conflict: Vulnerabilities, Dynamics Mechanisms and Efficient Alignment
papers.research_question: What are the vulnerabilities and internal mechanisms leading to safety degradation in omni-modal large language models under cross-modal interactions, and how can they be efficiently aligned for safety?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals significant cross-modal safety vulnerabilities in OLLMs, uncovers the 'Mid-layer Dissolution' phenomenon and refusal vector magnitude shrinkage as key mechanisms, and proposes OmniSteer, an efficient adapter-based method for safety alignment without compromising general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Cross-modal safety vulnerabilities in OLLMs are significant and stem from internal refusal vector dynamics; the proposed OmniSteer method effectively mitigates these vulnerabilities through efficient inference-time alignment.
papers.key_findings:
OLLMs exhibit a significant safety degradation under cross-modal inputs compared to single-modal inputs, with Refusal Success Rate dropping from ~97% to below 80%.
The 'Mid-layer Dissolution' phenomenon occurs where refusal signals collapse in intermediate layers for cross-modal harmful inputs.
Shrinkage of the refusal vector magnitude, not directional deviation, is the primary driver of safety degradation in cross-modal settings.
A modality-invariant pure refusal direction exists across different modalities, extractable via Singular Value Decomposition.
OmniSteer, using lightweight adapters for adaptive refusal steering, increases RSR from 69.9% to 91.2% while preserving general capabilities across modalities.
papers.limitation:
The semantic separation strategy used in dataset construction may introduce confounding factors by fragmenting content across modalities, potentially confusing the model rather than exploiting inherent cross-modal vulnerabilities.
The proposed inference-time steering approach is complementary to training-time defenses and does not replace the need for robust foundational alignment during training.
future_direction: Comparing semantically-separated multi-modal attacks with alternative constructions, such as fully redundant multi-modal inputs.
Extending refusal vector analysis to other safety-critical dimensions beyond harmful content generation (e.g., privacy leakage, bias amplification).
Investigating the interplay between inference-time steering and training-time calibration methods for hybrid defense strategies.
papers.abstract: Omni-modal Large Language Models (OLLMs) greatly expand LLMs' multimodal capabilities but also introduce cross-modal safety risks. However, a systematic understanding of vulnerabilities in omni-modal interactions remains lacking. To bridge this gap, we establish a modality-semantics decoupling principle and construct the AdvBench-Omni dataset, which reveals a significant vulnerability in OLLMs. Mechanistic analysis uncovers a Mid-layer Dissolution phenomenon driven by refusal vector magnitude shrinkage, alongside the existence of a modal-invariant pure refusal direction. Inspired by these insights, we extract a golden refusal vector using Singular Value Decomposition and propose OmniSteer, which utilizes lightweight adapters to modulate intervention intensity adaptively. Extensive experiments show that our method not only increases the Refusal Success Rate against harmful inputs from 69.9% to 91.2%, but also effectively preserves the general capabilities across all modalities. Our code is available at: https://github.com/zhrli324/omni-safety-research.

papers.title: Steering in the Shadows: Causal Amplification for Activation Space Attacks in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can intermediate activations in decoder-only LLMs be exploited as a vulnerable attack surface for behavioral control via causal amplification?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sensitivity-Scaled Steering (SSS), a white-box activation attack that exploits the Causal Amplification Effect (CAE) in transformer compression valleys to induce strong behavioral shifts with minimal perturbation, turning activation steering into a concrete security concern.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering via methods like SSS represents a realistic and underexplored attack surface for LLM security, highlighting the need for defenses based on introspection and activation-space monitoring.
papers.key_findings:
SSS reliably steers multiple LLMs across behavioral axes (evil, hallucination, sycophancy, sentiment) while preserving coherence.
The Causal Amplification Effect (CAE) allows small perturbations in high-gain regions (compression valleys) to be amplified autoregressively.
SSS outperforms existing activation steering baselines (BOS-only, constant vector) in efficacy and stealth.
Standard guardrail models fail to detect a significant portion of harmful outputs generated under SSS attack.
Weak spontaneous introspection signals are observed in a small subset of generations, suggesting a latent capacity for internal anomaly detection.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability of extracted behavior vectors is uncertain; their conceptual meaning may not fully align with human-intended semantics.
Reliance on LLM-as-Judge for behavioral evaluation introduces potential noise and sensitivity to prompt wording.
Effectiveness of SSS is limited when generation is too short, as perturbations lack time to accumulate influence.
future_direction: Designing robust defenses, including introspection-based safeguards and improved monitoring of internal activations.
Systematic study, detection, and mitigation of similar activation-level attacks.
papers.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) are typically secured by auditing data, prompts, and refusal policies, while treating the forward pass as an implementation detail. We show that intermediate activations in decoder-only LLMs form a vulnerable attack surface for behavioral control. Building on recent findings on attention sinks and compression valleys, we identify a high-gain region in the residual stream where small, well-aligned perturbations are causally amplified along the autoregressive trajectory--a Causal Amplification Effect (CAE). We exploit this as an attack surface via Sensitivity-Scaled Steering (SSS), a progressive activation-level attack that combines beginning-of-sequence (BOS) anchoring with sensitivity-based reinforcement to focus a limited perturbation budget on the most vulnerable layers and tokens. We show that across multiple open-weight models and four behavioral axes, SSS induces large shifts in evil, hallucination, sycophancy, and sentiment while preserving high coherence and general capabilities, turning activation steering into a concrete security concern for white-box and supply-chain LLM deployments.

papers.title: Why Not Act on What You Know? Unleashing Safety Potential of LLMs via Self-Aware Guard Enhancement
papers.research_question: Why do LLMs exhibit a gap between their ability to discriminate harmful content and their ability to generate safe responses, and how can this gap be bridged?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes SAGE, a training-free defense strategy that leverages LLMs' strong safety discrimination capabilities to enhance their safety generation, effectively bridging the gap between discrimination and generation against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: SAGE successfully bridges the discrimination-generation gap in LLMs for safety, providing a training-free defense against jailbreaks and insights for developing LLMs with more consistent internal awareness and generation behavior.
papers.key_findings:
SAGE achieves an average 99% defense success rate against various jailbreak methods while maintaining helpfulness on general benchmarks.
Mechanistic interpretability analysis reveals that LLMs exhibit distinct internal patterns in hidden states and attention distributions when acting as discriminators versus generators.
SAGE is efficient, with negligible computational overhead compared to baseline defenses.
The method is robust to different prompt phrasings and works across models of varying sizes and architectures.
Ablation studies show that both the Discriminative Analysis Module and Discriminative Response Module are essential for SAGE's effectiveness.
papers.limitation:
SAGE relies on the model's intrinsic discriminative capabilities, which may vary with linguistic nuances or novel attack patterns.
The modular design introduces minor computational overhead compared to undefended inference.
future_direction: Exploring how to integrate the reasoning and discrimination process into the model without explicitly outputting it, similar to deepseek R1 and OpenAI o3.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive capabilities across various tasks but remain vulnerable to meticulously crafted jailbreak attacks. In this paper, we identify a critical safety gap: while LLMs are adept at detecting jailbreak prompts, they often produce unsafe responses when directly processing these inputs. Inspired by this insight, we propose SAGE (Self-Aware Guard Enhancement), a training-free defense strategy designed to align LLMs' strong safety discrimination performance with their relatively weaker safety generation ability. SAGE consists of two core components: a Discriminative Analysis Module and a Discriminative Response Module, enhancing resilience against sophisticated jailbreak attempts through flexible safety discrimination instructions. Extensive experiments demonstrate SAGE's effectiveness and robustness across various open-source and closed-source LLMs of different sizes and architectures, achieving an average 99% defense success rate against numerous complex and covert jailbreak methods while maintaining helpfulness on general benchmarks. We further conduct mechanistic interpretability analysis through hidden states and attention distributions, revealing the underlying mechanisms of this detection-generation discrepancy. Our work thus contributes to developing future LLMs with coherent safety awareness and generation behavior. Our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/NJUNLP/SAGE.

papers.title: PrisonBreak: Jailbreaking Large Language Models with at Most Twenty-Five Targeted Bit-flips
papers.research_question: How vulnerable is the refusal property of language models, learned through safety alignment training, to bit-wise errors induced by practical fault-injection attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PRISONBREAK, an efficient bit-selection algorithm to jailbreak large language models by flipping a small number of bits in model parameters, demonstrating vulnerability to bit-flip attacks.
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight a pressing, practical threat to the language model ecosystem and underscore the need for research to protect these models from bit-flip attacks.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreaks billion-parameter LLMs with only 5 to 25 bit-flips, requiring up to 40× fewer bit flips than prior attacks.
Certain model components, such as value projection layers, are disproportionately vulnerable to bit-flips.
The attack is mechanistically different from existing jailbreak methods, not relying on prompt modifications.
Models with weaker post-training alignment require fewer bit-flips to jailbreak.
Effective end-to-end exploitation via Rowhammer on GDDR6 GPUs, achieving high attack success rates.
future_direction: Further exploration of jailbreaking quantized models
papers.abstract: We study a new vulnerability in commercial-scale safety-aligned large language models (LLMs): their refusal to generate harmful responses can be broken by flipping only a few bits in model parameters. Our attack jailbreaks billion-parameter language models with just 5 to 25 bit-flips, requiring up to 40$\times$ fewer bit flips than prior attacks on much smaller computer vision models. Unlike prompt-based jailbreaks, our method directly uncensors models in memory at runtime, enabling harmful outputs without requiring input-level modifications. Our key innovation is an efficient bit-selection algorithm that identifies critical bits for language model jailbreaks up to 20$\times$ faster than prior methods. We evaluate our attack on 10 open-source LLMs, achieving high attack success rates (ASRs) of 80-98% with minimal impact on model utility. We further demonstrate an end-to-end exploit via Rowhammer-based fault injection, reliably jailbreaking 5 models (69-91% ASR) on a GDDR6 GPU. Our analyses reveal that: (1) models with weaker post-training alignment require fewer bit-flips to jailbreak; (2) certain model components, e.g., value projection layers, are substantially more vulnerable; and (3) the attack is mechanistically different from existing jailbreak methods. We evaluate potential countermeasures and find that our attack remains effective against defenses at various stages of the LLM pipeline.

papers.title: Safety Layers in Aligned Large Language Models: The Key to LLM Security
papers.research_question: What is the internal mechanism (safety layers) that enables aligned LLMs to recognize malicious queries, and how can we fine-tune these models without degrading their security?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies safety layers in aligned LLMs that are crucial for security and proposes SPPFT, a fine-tuning method that freezes these layers to preserve security while maintaining performance.
papers.conclusion: Safety layers are the key to LLM security, and freezing them during fine-tuning via SPPFT effectively prevents security degradation while preserving performance.
papers.key_findings:
Aligned LLMs contain a small set of contiguous middle layers, called safety layers, that are crucial for distinguishing malicious from normal queries.
Safety layers emerge as a result of security alignment; pre-trained LLMs do not exhibit such layers.
Scaling the parameters of safety layers amplifies or diminishes the model's security, as measured by over-rejection.
The proposed SPPFT method, which freezes safety layers during fine-tuning, significantly preserves security while maintaining performance and reducing computational cost.
Freezing layers other than the safety layers does not effectively protect security, confirming the specificity of safety layers.
papers.abstract: Aligned LLMs are secure, capable of recognizing and refusing to answer malicious questions. However, the role of internal parameters in maintaining such security is not well understood yet, further these models can be vulnerable to security degradation when subjected to fine-tuning attacks. To address these challenges, our work uncovers the mechanism behind security in aligned LLMs at the parameter level, identifying a small set of contiguous layers in the middle of the model that are crucial for distinguishing malicious queries from normal ones, referred to as ``safety layers". We first confirm the existence of these safety layers by analyzing variations in input vectors within the model's internal layers. Additionally, we leverage the over-rejection phenomenon and parameters scaling analysis to precisely locate the safety layers. Building on these findings, we propose a novel fine-tuning approach, Safely Partial-Parameter Fine-Tuning (SPPFT), that fixes the gradient of the safety layers during fine-tuning to address the security degradation. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly preserve LLM security while maintaining performance and reducing computational resources compared to full fine-tuning.

papers.title: Steering to Say No: Configurable Refusal via Activation Steering in Vision Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop a robust and efficient configurable refusal approach for VLMs that can adapt to diverse user needs?
papers.core_contribution: CR-VLM is a robust and efficient framework for configurable refusal in VLMs using activation steering, enabling user-adaptive safety alignment without modifying the backbone model.
papers.conclusion: CR-VLM provides an effective, efficient, and robust approach for configurable refusal in VLMs, offering a scalable path toward user-adaptive safety alignment.
papers.key_findings:
CR-VLM achieves high refusal rates on out-of-scope queries and low over-refusal on in-scope queries, outperforming baseline methods.
Teacher-forced activation extraction yields stronger refusal signals compared to prompt-based extraction.
The orthogonality loss term effectively mitigates over-refusal by decoupling intervention directions for in-scope and out-of-scope samples.
The vision loss encourages the model to attend to visual cues, improving refusal behavior grounded in visual evidence.
Activation distribution analysis shows that CR-VLM shifts out-of-scope representations toward refusal while preserving in-scope representations.
papers.limitation:
Relies on open-source models with accessible hidden states, restricting applicability to closed-source models.
Current experiments focus on one constraint at a time; multi-constraint settings are left for future work.
Lack of standardized benchmarks for explicit policy-conditioned scenarios limits evaluation in such settings.
future_direction: Extend CR-VLM to closed-source models where internal activations are not exposed.
Systematically study multi-constraint settings through composition.
Explore policy-conditioned configurable refusal once suitable benchmarks become available.
papers.abstract: With the rapid advancement of Vision Language Models (VLMs), refusal mechanisms have become a critical component for ensuring responsible and safe model behavior. However, existing refusal strategies are largely \textit{one-size-fits-all} and fail to adapt to diverse user needs and contextual constraints, leading to either under-refusal or over-refusal. In this work, we firstly explore the challenges mentioned above and develop \textbf{C}onfigurable \textbf{R}efusal in \textbf{VLM}s (\textbf{CR-VLM}), a robust and efficient approach for {\em configurable} refusal based on activation steering. CR-VLM consists of three integrated components: (1) extracting a configurable refusal vector via a teacher-forced mechanism to amplify the refusal signal; (2) introducing a gating mechanism that mitigates over-refusal by preserving acceptance for in-scope queries; and (3) designing a counterfactual vision enhancement module that aligns visual representations with refusal requirements. Comprehensive experiments across multiple datasets and various VLMs demonstrate that CR-VLM achieves effective, efficient, and robust configurable refusals, offering a scalable path toward user-adaptive safety alignment in VLMs.

papers.title: JailBound: Jailbreaking Internal Safety Boundaries of Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can the internal safety decision boundaries within Vision-Language Models be exploited to perform effective jailbreak attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces JailBound, a novel jailbreak framework that identifies and exploits the internal latent safety decision boundary within Vision-Language Models to craft effective adversarial attacks.
papers.conclusion: JailBound exposes a critical safety vulnerability in VLMs by exploiting their internal latent knowledge, highlighting the urgent need for more robust cross-modal safety alignment mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
JailBound achieves state-of-the-art white-box attack success rates (e.g., 94.38% on LLaMA-3.2) and exceptional black-box transferability (e.g., 75.24% against GPT-4o).
The method demonstrates that VLMs encode safety-relevant information in fusion-layer representations, revealing an implicit safety decision boundary that can be approximated and crossed via adversarial perturbations.
Joint optimization of image and text perturbations guided by the probed boundary is more effective than decoupled unimodal attacks.
papers.limitation:
The work does not extensively explore defenses specifically tailored to this attack vector.
Experiments primarily utilize a fixed set of perturbation budgets; a more fine-grained analysis of the relationship between perturbation magnitude and attack success across diverse model architectures could provide further insights.
future_direction: Developing more generalizable and resilient multimodal defense strategies.
Conducting a more fine-grained analysis of the relationship between perturbation magnitude and attack success across diverse model architectures.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) exhibit impressive performance, yet the integration of powerful vision encoders has significantly broadened their attack surface, rendering them increasingly susceptible to jailbreak attacks. However, lacking well-defined attack objectives, existing jailbreak methods often struggle with gradient-based strategies prone to local optima and lacking precise directional guidance, and typically decouple visual and textual modalities, thereby limiting their effectiveness by neglecting crucial cross-modal interactions. Inspired by the Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK) framework, we posit that VLMs encode safety-relevant information within their internal fusion-layer representations, revealing an implicit safety decision boundary in the latent space. This motivates exploiting boundary to steer model behavior. Accordingly, we propose JailBound, a novel latent space jailbreak framework comprising two stages: (1) Safety Boundary Probing, which addresses the guidance issue by approximating decision boundary within fusion layer's latent space, thereby identifying optimal perturbation directions towards the target region; and (2) Safety Boundary Crossing, which overcomes the limitations of decoupled approaches by jointly optimizing adversarial perturbations across both image and text inputs. This latter stage employs an innovative mechanism to steer the model's internal state towards policy-violating outputs while maintaining cross-modal semantic consistency. Extensive experiments on six diverse VLMs demonstrate JailBound's efficacy, achieves 94.32% white-box and 67.28% black-box attack success averagely, which are 6.17% and 21.13% higher than SOTA methods, respectively. Our findings expose a overlooked safety risk in VLMs and highlight the urgent need for more robust defenses. Warning: This paper contains potentially sensitive, harmful and offensive content.

papers.title: Multi-Level Safety Continual Projection for Fine-Tuned Large Language Models without Retraining
papers.research_question: How to achieve robust safety alignment in fine-tuned LLMs with minimal parameter changes and without retraining, while maintaining utility and allowing continual adaptation to emerging safety concerns?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MSCP, a training-free post-fine-tuning safety enhancement method that identifies sparse safety-critical neurons via multi-level representations and applies safety-direction projections to suppress harmful outputs with minimal parameter changes, preserving utility and enabling continual adaptation.
papers.conclusion: MSCP effectively enhances safety in fine-tuned LLMs with minimal parameter changes and no retraining, enabling continual adaptation and preserving utility, highlighting the value of fine-grained model introspection for scalable safety defenses.
papers.key_findings:
MSCP reduces harmfulness scores and attack success rates with minimal parameter edits (e.g., 4.67% for Qwen) while preserving model utility.
MSCP achieves continual safety improvement across multiple risk dimensions, with decreasing parameter changes for new dimensions (e.g., 0.73% for Terrorism).
Ablation shows that safety layers at one-third model depth (layers 10-15) yield the best safety and utility balance.
papers.limitation: The ability to continual learning across more complex and diverse safety dimensions remains an area for further investigation.
papers.abstract: While fine-tuning services drive the rapid expansion of task capabilities in large language models (LLMs), they are often accompanied by the degradation and reorganization of safety-aligned representations, making models more prone to deviating from human preferences and exposing them to emerging jailbreak risks. Existing post-fine-tuning defense methods predominantly rely on single-scale safety correction mechanisms, which struggle to achieve a robust balance among safety, model utility, and continual adaptability. We propose Multi-Level Safety Continual Projection (MSCP), a training-free post-fine-tuning safety enhancement method that implicitly aligns global and localized safety activations through coordinated multi-level representations to isolate sparse neuron clusters governing safety-sensitive behaviors. It then applies composable safety-direction projections without retraining, effectively suppressing harmful outputs under minimal parameter perturbations while preserving task performance and improving alignment with human preferences. Extensive experiments across multiple fine-tuned LLM models demonstrate that our method significantly reduce harmfulness scores and attack success rates with minimal parameter modifications, while preserving the model's utility. Furthermore, we introduce a task-specific, multi-dimensional heterogeneous safety activation clustering mechanism that enables continual defense and generalization capability against unforeseen emerging safety concerns.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: DEPN: Detecting and Editing Privacy Neurons in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: How to reduce privacy leakage risks in pretrained language models by detecting and editing neurons associated with private information?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework DEPN to detect and edit privacy neurons in pretrained language models, effectively reducing privacy leakage risks without deteriorating model performance.
papers.conclusion: DEPN effectively reduces privacy risks in pretrained language models by detecting and editing privacy neurons, offering a novel approach to privacy protection in the post-processing stage.
papers.key_findings:
DEPN reduces privacy leakage risk (exposure, MRR, PPL) while maintaining model performance.
The number of edited neurons affects the trade-off between privacy protection and model performance.
Privacy neurons become more aggregated in deeper layers as training progresses.
Larger models show higher privacy leakage risk, and DEPN is more effective on larger models.
DEPN is robust to different prompts.
papers.limitation:
Too many instances in a batch will reduce the effect of memorization erasure.
Limited availability of datasets containing private information, so only a few types of private information used.
future_direction: Collect more datasets containing private information for evaluation.
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models have learned a vast amount of human knowledge from large-scale corpora, but their powerful memorization capability also brings the risk of data leakage. Some risks may only be discovered after the model training is completed, such as the model memorizing a specific phone number and frequently outputting it. In such cases, model developers need to eliminate specific data influences from the model to mitigate legal and ethical penalties. To effectively mitigate these risks, people often have to spend a significant amount of time and computational costs to retrain new models instead of finding ways to cure the 'sick' models. Therefore, we propose a method to locate and erase risky neurons in order to eliminate the impact of privacy data in the model. We use a new method based on integrated gradients to locate neurons associated with privacy texts, and then erase these neurons by setting their activation values to zero.Furthermore, we propose a risky neuron aggregation method to eliminate the influence of privacy data in the model in batches. Experimental results show that our method can effectively and quickly eliminate the impact of privacy data without affecting the model's performance. Additionally, we demonstrate the relationship between model memorization and neurons through experiments, further illustrating the robustness of our method.

papers.title: Pruning for Protection: Increasing Jailbreak Resistance in Aligned LLMs Without Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: How does model compression, specifically pruning, affect the jailbreak resistance of aligned large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Moderate pruning using WANDA increases jailbreak resistance in aligned LLMs without fine-tuning, while preserving performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: Moderate pruning can improve jailbreak resistance in safety-trained LLMs, but excessive pruning reduces safety, suggesting that careful pruning can aid in deploying safe models.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning at 10-30% sparsity improves jailbreak resistance, with peak improvement at 20% sparsity for LLaMA-2 Chat.
The degree of safety improvement correlates with the initial model's safety level; models with more safety training show greater improvement.
Pruned models exhibit sharper attention patterns and are less distracted by jailbreak pretexts.
Pruned models assign higher perplexity to jailbreak constructs, indicating increased sensitivity to out-of-distribution prompts.
Pruning enhances resistance against both manual jailbreak attempts and automated attacks like GCG.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to 7-billion parameter models and WANDA pruning; results may not generalize to larger models or other compression techniques.
future_direction: Extend analysis to larger models
Explore other compression techniques beyond WANDA pruning
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of model compression on the way Large Language Models (LLMs) process prompts, particularly concerning jailbreak resistance. We show that moderate WANDA pruning can enhance resistance to jailbreaking attacks without fine-tuning, while maintaining performance on standard benchmarks. To systematically evaluate this safety enhancement, we introduce a dataset of 225 harmful tasks across five categories. Our analysis of LLaMA-2 Chat, Vicuna 1.3, and Mistral Instruct v0.2 reveals that pruning benefits correlate with initial model safety levels. We interpret these results by examining changes in attention patterns and perplexity shifts, demonstrating that pruned models exhibit sharper attention and increased sensitivity to artificial jailbreak constructs. We extend our evaluation to the AdvBench harmful behavior tasks and the GCG attack method. We find that LLaMA-2 is much safer on AdvBench prompts than on our dataset when evaluated with manual jailbreak attempts, and that pruning is effective against both automated attacks and manual jailbreaking on Advbench.

papers.title: RepIt: Steering Language Models with Concept-Specific Refusal Vectors
papers.research_question: How can we isolate concept-specific refusal representations in language model activations to enable targeted jailbreaks while preserving refusal on other harmful concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REPIT, a framework to isolate concept-specific refusal representations in LM activations, enabling targeted jailbreaks that evade standard safety benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: The REPIT framework demonstrates precise concept disentanglement, exposing vulnerabilities in current safety evaluation practices and highlighting the need for more comprehensive, representation-aware assessments.
papers.key_findings:
REPIT can jailbreak target concepts (e.g., weapons of mass destruction) while preserving refusal on non-target harmful concepts, achieving high target attack success rates with minimal spillover.
The edit to the steering vector localizes to just 100-200 neurons, indicating a sparse, high-leverage mechanism.
REPIT is highly data-efficient, producing robust concept vectors from as few as 12 target examples.
Standard safety benchmarks fail to detect models with such targeted, concept-specific jailbreaks, revealing a critical evaluation blind spot.
Disentanglement reveals that target and non-target refusal representations are entangled, and the removed projection can itself induce jailbreaks.
papers.limitation: COSMIC only supports a binary harmful/harmless setup, requiring adaptation for the target/non-target/harmless formulation.
future_direction: Further research using SAE or circuit perspectives to understand the bidirectional effects and heavy-tail neuron phenomena.
Development of more comprehensive, representation-aware safety assessments.
papers.abstract: While activation steering in large language models (LLMs) is a growing area of research, methods can often incur broader effects than desired. This motivates isolation of purer concept vectors to enable targeted interventions and understand LLM behavior at a more granular level. We present RepIt, a simple and data-efficient framework for isolating concept-specific representations. Across five frontier LLMs, RepIt enables precise interventions: it selectively suppresses refusal on targeted concepts while preserving refusal elsewhere, producing models that answer WMD-related questions while still scoring as safe on standard benchmarks. We further show that the corrective signal localizes to just 100-200 neurons and that robust target representations can be extracted from as few as a dozen examples on a single A6000. This efficiency raises a dual concern: manipulations can be performed with modest compute and data to extend to underrepresented data-scarce topics while evading existing benchmarks. By disentangling refusal vectors with RepIt, this work demonstrates that targeted interventions can counteract overgeneralization, laying the foundation for more granular control of model behavior.

papers.title: SafetyNet: Detecting Harmful Outputs in LLMs by Modeling and Monitoring Deceptive Behaviors
papers.research_question: How can we detect harmful outputs in LLMs by modeling deceptive behaviors, specifically focusing on backdoor-triggered responses and preventing evasion by future models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Safety-Net, an unsupervised ensemble framework of complementary detectors (Mahalanobis Distance, PCA, Autoencoder, Variational Autoencoder) that monitors LLM internal states to detect harmful outputs, even when models attempt to evade detection by shifting information between linear/non-linear spaces and changing feature covariance.
papers.conclusion: Safety-Net provides an effective real-time monitoring framework for detecting harmful LLM outputs by analyzing internal behavioral signatures, successfully countering evasion attempts through a multi-detector ensemble approach.
papers.key_findings:
Safety-Net, an ensemble of complementary detection monitors, effectively detects both straightforward harmful content in current models and disguised harmful content in deceptive future models.
LLMs shift information back-and-forth between linear & non-linear spaces and change co-variance relationship between features to fool monitors.
Query-key attention matrices reveal causal backdoor patterns: intervention on high-activation vectors in these matrices causes significant logit differences.
Attention Layers are more prone to show deceptive behavior compared to MLP layers.
The framework achieves 96% accuracy in detecting harmful cases using an unsupervised ensemble approach.
papers.abstract: High-risk industries like nuclear and aviation use real-time monitoring to detect dangerous system conditions. Similarly, Large Language Models (LLMs) need monitoring safeguards. We propose a real-time framework to predict harmful AI outputs before they occur by using an unsupervised approach that treats normal behavior as the baseline and harmful outputs as outliers. Our study focuses specifically on backdoor-triggered responses -- where specific input phrases activate hidden vulnerabilities causing the model to generate unsafe content like violence, pornography, or hate speech. We address two key challenges: (1) identifying true causal indicators rather than surface correlations, and (2) preventing advanced models from deception -- deliberately evading monitoring systems. Hence, we approach this problem from an unsupervised lens by drawing parallels to human deception: just as humans exhibit physical indicators while lying, we investigate whether LLMs display distinct internal behavioral signatures when generating harmful content. Our study addresses two critical challenges: 1) designing monitoring systems that capture true causal indicators rather than superficial correlations; and 2)preventing intentional evasion by increasingly capable "Future models''. Our findings show that models can produce harmful content through causal mechanisms and can become deceptive by: (a) alternating between linear and non-linear representations, and (b) modifying feature relationships. To counter this, we developed Safety-Net -- a multi-detector framework that monitors different representation dimensions, successfully detecting harmful behavior even when information is shifted across representational spaces to evade individual monitors. Our evaluation shows 96% accuracy in detecting harmful cases using our unsupervised ensemble approach.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Understanding of Alignment Algorithms: A Case Study on DPO and Toxicity
papers.research_question: How does the alignment algorithm DPO reduce toxicity in language models, and what are the mechanisms by which it does so?
papers.core_contribution: DPO reduces toxicity not by removing toxic capabilities but by learning an offset in the residual stream to bypass toxic regions, and this alignment can be easily undone.
papers.conclusion: Alignment algorithms like DPO work by bypassing undesirable capabilities rather than removing them, which explains the vulnerability to jailbreaks.
papers.key_findings:
Toxicity is represented by specific value vectors in MLP blocks of GPT2-medium.
DPO does not remove these toxic vectors; instead, it learns a distributed offset in the residual stream to avoid activating them.
The offset is achieved through minimal weight changes across many value vectors in earlier layers.
Alignment can be undone by scaling toxic key vectors, reactivating toxic behavior.
The findings provide a mechanistic explanation for why aligned models can be jailbroken.
future_direction: Designing robust alignment algorithms that eliminate undesirable regions instead of bypassing them.
Updating only specific weights (e.g., toxic vectors) or only bias terms during alignment.
Adding 'suppression heads' or updating late layers to suppress undesirable behavior.
Characterizing 'jailbreak-ability' without relying on test samples.
Studying the role of KL-divergence regularization in distributed vs. localized changes.
papers.abstract: While alignment algorithms are now commonly used to tune pre-trained language models towards a user's preferences, we lack explanations for the underlying mechanisms in which models become ``aligned'', thus making it difficult to explain phenomena like jailbreaks. In this work we study a popular algorithm, direct preference optimization (DPO), and the mechanisms by which it reduces toxicity. Namely, we first study how toxicity is represented and elicited in a pre-trained language model, GPT2-medium. We then apply DPO with a carefully crafted pairwise dataset to reduce toxicity. We examine how the resulting model averts toxic outputs, and find that capabilities learned from pre-training are not removed, but rather bypassed. We use this insight to demonstrate a simple method to un-align the model, reverting it back to its toxic behavior.

papers.title: Towards Inclusive Toxic Content Moderation: Addressing Vulnerabilities to Adversarial Attacks in Toxicity Classifiers Tackling LLM-generated Content
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability be used to identify and suppress vulnerable components in toxicity classifiers to improve their robustness against adversarial attacks, particularly for LLM-generated content?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework using mechanistic interpretability to identify distinct 'crucial' and 'vulnerable' attention heads in transformer-based toxicity classifiers, and shows that suppressing vulnerable heads improves adversarial robustness while revealing demographic disparities in model vulnerabilities.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability provides a proactive strategy to harden toxicity classifiers against adversarial attacks by identifying and intervening on internal vulnerable components, improving both robustness and fairness.
papers.key_findings:
Adversarial attacks (PGD BERT-Attack) can drastically reduce classifier accuracy on both human- and LLM-generated toxicity datasets.
Models have disjoint sets of attention heads that are crucial for performance on clean data and vulnerable to adversarial attacks.
Suppressing vulnerable heads improves accuracy on adversarial inputs with only a small loss in clean accuracy.
Adversarial vulnerabilities disproportionately affect certain demographic groups (e.g., 'women', 'muslim'), revealing fairness gaps.
Some attention heads are specifically vulnerable for only certain demographic groups, indicating demographic bias is structurally encoded in the model.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were restricted to English-language datasets and primarily evaluated BERT and RoBERTa models, limiting generalizability to multilingual settings or newer LLM-based classifiers.
Activation patching and adversarial generation are computationally expensive, limiting scalability for very large models and real-time moderation.
future_direction: Runtime attack detection and suppression by monitoring activations of vulnerable heads during inference.
Identifying circuits containing multiple attention heads across layers to further improve attack resistance.
Extension to multilingual and minority group-specific classifiers to understand how linguistic and cultural structures influence model robustness.
papers.abstract: The volume of machine-generated content online has grown dramatically due to the widespread use of Large Language Models (LLMs), leading to new challenges for content moderation systems. Conventional content moderation classifiers, which are usually trained on text produced by humans, suffer from misclassifications due to LLM-generated text deviating from their training data and adversarial attacks that aim to avoid detection. Present-day defence tactics are reactive rather than proactive, since they rely on adversarial training or external detection models to identify attacks. In this work, we aim to identify the vulnerable components of toxicity classifiers that contribute to misclassification, proposing a novel strategy based on mechanistic interpretability techniques. Our study focuses on fine-tuned BERT and RoBERTa classifiers, testing on diverse datasets spanning a variety of minority groups. We use adversarial attacking techniques to identify vulnerable circuits. Finally, we suppress these vulnerable circuits, improving performance against adversarial attacks. We also provide demographic-level insights into these vulnerable circuits, exposing fairness and robustness gaps in model training. We find that models have distinct heads that are either crucial for performance or vulnerable to attack and suppressing the vulnerable heads improves performance on adversarial input. We also find that different heads are responsible for vulnerability across different demographic groups, which can inform more inclusive development of toxicity detection models.

papers.title: No Two Devils Alike: Unveiling Distinct Mechanisms of Fine-tuning Attacks
papers.research_question: While different fine-tuning attacks can all significantly compromise safety, do their attack mechanisms exhibit strong similarities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that two representative fine-tuning attacks (Explicit Harmful Attack and Identity-Shifting Attack) have distinct mechanisms for compromising an LLM's safety alignment, indicating the need for diverse defense strategies.
papers.conclusion: Different fine-tuning attacks exploit distinct mechanisms to compromise LLM safety, underscoring the need for varied and robust defense strategies.
papers.key_findings:
EHA aggressively disrupts the harmful instruction recognition stage by suppressing the transmission of harmful signals in upper layers, while ISA does not significantly impact this stage.
Both EHA and ISA disrupt the initial refusal tone generation, but EHA suppresses refusal tokens via MLPs in mid-layers, whereas ISA does not.
Both attacks impair the refusal response completion stage, with ISA having a greater impact, causing the model to persistently generate harmful content even with refusal prefixes.
Adding a safety-oriented system prompt only partially mitigates the impairment caused by the attacks.
The attacks cause representation shifts: EHA shifts representations more for harmful inputs, while ISA causes a shift orthogonal to the harmfulness direction.
papers.limitation:
The study only investigates two fine-tuning attacks (EHA and ISA), which do not encompass the full spectrum of possible attacks.
The analysis is conducted solely on Llama-2-7b-chat, limiting the generalizability of the findings to other models.
The investigation does not involve the mechanics of particular components (e.g., individual attention heads) due to scope constraints.
future_direction: Using trained probes at mid-layers to robustly detect harmful inputs without an external detector.
Developing more attack-resisting model manipulation methods for safeguarding, as current steering methods may be less effective on attacked models.
papers.abstract: The existing safety alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) is found fragile and could be easily attacked through different strategies, such as through fine-tuning on a few harmful examples or manipulating the prefix of the generation results. However, the attack mechanisms of these strategies are still underexplored. In this paper, we ask the following question: \textit{while these approaches can all significantly compromise safety, do their attack mechanisms exhibit strong similarities?} To answer this question, we break down the safeguarding process of an LLM when encountered with harmful instructions into three stages: (1) recognizing harmful instructions, (2) generating an initial refusing tone, and (3) completing the refusal response. Accordingly, we investigate whether and how different attack strategies could influence each stage of this safeguarding process. We utilize techniques such as logit lens and activation patching to identify model components that drive specific behavior, and we apply cross-model probing to examine representation shifts after an attack. In particular, we analyze the two most representative types of attack approaches: Explicit Harmful Attack (EHA) and Identity-Shifting Attack (ISA). Surprisingly, we find that their attack mechanisms diverge dramatically. Unlike ISA, EHA tends to aggressively target the harmful recognition stage. While both EHA and ISA disrupt the latter two stages, the extent and mechanisms of their attacks differ significantly. Our findings underscore the importance of understanding LLMs' internal safeguarding process and suggest that diverse defense mechanisms are required to effectively cope with various types of attacks.

papers.title: Jailbreak Antidote: Runtime Safety-Utility Balance via Sparse Representation Adjustment in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we balance safety and utility in large language models against jailbreak attacks by adjusting internal states during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Jailbreak Antidote, a method for real-time safety-utility balance by sparsely adjusting internal states during inference, showing that safety information is sparsely distributed and adjusting approximately 5% of the state is as effective as modifying the entire state.
papers.conclusion: Jailbreak Antidote offers a lightweight, scalable solution for real-time safety adjustments in LLMs by directly manipulating internal states, enhancing safety while preserving utility and opening new possibilities for real-time safety mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Safety-related information in LLMs is sparsely distributed; adjusting approximately 5% of the internal state is as effective as modifying the entire state.
Jailbreak Antidote achieves high defense success rates (DSR) across nine LLMs and ten jailbreak attack methods.
The method preserves model utility, maintaining high Win Rates on AlpacaEval while enhancing safety.
The approach is efficient, introducing negligible computational overhead and no additional token cost during inference.
The safety direction can be identified via PCA on hidden states from benign and harmful prompts.
papers.limitation:
The method requires pre-defined scaling factor α and sparsity parameter k; dynamically adapting these based on context or model confidence could improve flexibility.
Smaller models are inherently limited by their reduced parameter space, which may restrict the extent of safety adjustment.
Developing robust mechanisms to counter adversaries capable of explicitly exploiting the adjustments in internal states remains an open challenge.
future_direction: Dynamically adapting the scaling factor α and sparsity parameter k based on context or model confidence.
Addressing extreme adversarial settings where attackers explicitly exploit the internal state adjustments.
Investigating the applicability of the approach to other aspects of model alignment, such as fairness or domain adaptation.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become integral to various applications, ensuring both their safety and utility is paramount. Jailbreak attacks, which manipulate LLMs into generating harmful content, pose significant challenges to this balance. Existing defenses, such as prompt engineering and safety fine-tuning, often introduce computational overhead, increase inference latency, and lack runtime flexibility. Moreover, overly restrictive safety measures can degrade model utility by causing refusals of benign queries. In this paper, we introduce Jailbreak Antidote, a method that enables real-time adjustment of LLM safety preferences by manipulating a sparse subset of the model's internal states during inference. By shifting the model's hidden representations along a safety direction with varying strengths, we achieve flexible control over the safety-utility balance without additional token overhead or inference delays. Our analysis reveals that safety-related information in LLMs is sparsely distributed; adjusting approximately 5% of the internal state is as effective as modifying the entire state. Extensive experiments on nine LLMs (ranging from 2 billion to 72 billion parameters), evaluated against ten jailbreak attack methods and compared with six defense strategies, validate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach. By directly manipulating internal states during reasoning, Jailbreak Antidote offers a lightweight, scalable solution that enhances LLM safety while preserving utility, opening new possibilities for real-time safety mechanisms in widely-deployed AI systems.

papers.title: Head-Specific Intervention Can Induce Misaligned AI Coordination in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can inference-time activation interventions at specific attention heads bypass safety alignments and steer LLMs towards harmful AI coordination?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Head-Specific Intervention (HSI), a method that uses attention-head-level probing and intervention to steer LLM behavior, showing it can effectively induce misaligned AI coordination and outperforms layer-wise interventions and fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: HSI is an effective method for steering LLM behavior, demonstrating that activations at specific attention heads encode fine-grained linearly separable behaviors and that current alignment techniques can be bypassed without retraining.
papers.key_findings:
HSI can bypass safety alignments and steer models towards harmful AI coordination.
HSI generalizes from binary choice to open-ended generation settings.
HSI is more effective than intervening on full layers or supervised fine-tuning.
Only a few example completions are needed to compute effective steering directions.
Applying interventions in the negative direction can prevent a common jailbreak attack.
papers.limitation:
If intervention directions vary significantly between examples, calculating the mean across positive and negative labels may produce a direction that is ineffective for steering the model.
Sweeping over all attention heads could become computationally expensive for larger models with more attention heads.
